R.q:
Follow the directions.

A clinic scheduler uses these steps to set a follow-up time. Start with 8:50 a.m. and carry out the steps in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Add 3 hours and 25 minutes.
2. If the time is now later than 12:00 noon, subtract 50 minutes; otherwise, add 50 minutes.
3. Move the time forward to the next quarter hour (:00, :15, :30 or :45), unless it is already on one.
4. Add 1 hour and 40 minutes.

What is the final time?
R.w: Step 1: 8:50 a.m. + 3:25 = 12:15 p.m. Step 2: 12:15 p.m. is later than noon, so subtract 50 minutes: 11:25 a.m. Step 3: forward to the next quarter hour: 11:30 a.m. Step 4: 11:30 a.m. + 1:40 = 1:10 p.m.

n.0: Takes the wrong branch in step 2 (adding 50 minutes to get 1:05 p.m.), then 1:15 p.m., then 2:55 p.m.
n.3: Rounds back to 11:15 a.m. in step 3 instead of forward to 11:30 a.m.

R.q:
Read the description of the map.

The map of Lake County uses a scale of 1 inch = 8 miles. On the map, the route from Pinecrest to the regional hospital in Millbrook measures 3.5 inches along Highway 12, shown as a solid red line. A county road between the same two towns measures 2.75 inches and is shown as a dashed black line. According to the legend, a dashed black line means "unpaved road, closed November through March." A compass rose shows north at the top of the map.

It is January. Based on the map, how many miles long is the shortest open route from Pinecrest to Millbrook?
o: 28 miles
22 miles
35 miles
24 miles
R.w: In January the dashed county road is closed, so the open route is Highway 12: 3.5 inches x 8 miles per inch = 28 miles.

n.1: 22 miles is the county road (2.75 x 8), which the legend shows is closed in January.
n.2: Applies a scale of 10 miles per inch instead of the map's 8 miles per inch.
n.3: Uses 3 inches instead of 3.5 inches for Highway 12.

R.q:
In a 12-week study, 60 adults who walked briskly for 30 minutes a day lowered their average resting heart rate from 76 to 70 beats per minute. A comparison group of 60 adults who kept their usual routines showed no change. After the study ended, researchers checked on the walkers for another 12 weeks. Walkers who stopped their daily walks returned to about their starting heart rates by the end of that period, while those who kept walking stayed near 70.

Lena was one of the walkers, and she plans to stop walking when the study ends. Based on the passage, what will most likely happen to her resting heart rate over the next 12 weeks?
o: It will probably stay near 70 because she completed the full 12 weeks of walking.
It will keep falling below 70 because the benefits of walking build over time.
It will rise above 76 because stopping exercise suddenly strains the heart.
It will probably drift back toward the rate she had before the study.
R.w: The follow-up found that walkers who stopped returned to about their starting heart rates within 12 weeks. Lena fits that group, so her rate should drift back toward where it began.

n.0: Staying near 70 applied to walkers who kept walking, not to those who stopped.
n.1: The passage shows no further drop after walking stops; this reverses the follow-up finding.
n.2: Walkers who stopped returned to about their starting rates; nothing suggests they rose above them.

R.q:
Last winter, a volunteer found a gray terrier curled in a roadside ditch, too weak to lift his head. We named him Biscuit. For three weeks, our staff fed him by hand every four hours and wrapped him in warm towels while he shivered through the nights. This morning, Biscuit trotted out the front door with his new family, tail wagging. Our shelter cares for about 400 animals a year. Every Biscuit begins with a donor like you. Please give today.

The author mainly tries to persuade readers by appealing to their
o: sense of logic, through data on the shelter's yearly costs
trust, through the shelter director's professional credentials
sense of duty, by comparing the shelter with other shelters
emotions, through a vivid story about a single rescued dog
R.w: Most of the letter tells Biscuit's story in moving detail (too weak to lift his head, shivering, tail wagging) before asking for money. That is mainly an appeal to emotion (pathos).

n.0: One figure appears (about 400 animals a year), but no cost data, and the story carries the appeal.
n.1: The letter never names its author's role or credentials.
n.2: No other shelters are mentioned.

R.q:
Daniela is writing a research paper on how well the shingles vaccine prevents shingles in adults over 50. Her instructor requires sources that are authoritative, current, and free of conflicts of interest, and warns that papers relying on personal stories or advertising will lose points. The paper is due in three weeks and must cite at least two sources on the vaccine's results. Daniela has gathered six possible sources.

Which sources meet her instructor's requirements? Select all that apply.
o: An online forum where adults describe side effects they experienced
A 1995 encyclopedia entry describing shingles and its symptoms
The CDC's current web page on how well the shingles vaccine works
A 2023 peer-reviewed study comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated adults
A magazine interview with an actor who received the vaccine
A television commercial produced by the vaccine's manufacturer
R.w: A recent peer-reviewed study is authoritative and current, and a federal public health agency's current page is authoritative with no product to sell. Both fit the instructor's criteria.

n.0: Forum posts are personal stories, which the instructor specifically warned against.
n.1: A 1995 entry is not current and cannot address how well today's vaccine works.
n.4: An actor's experience is anecdotal and is not expert evidence.
n.5: An advertisement from the manufacturer has a financial interest in the message.

R.q:
Read the passage and the student's summary.

Passage: Community fridges are refrigerators placed on sidewalks or outside businesses where anyone can leave or take food at any hour. Many appeared in U.S. cities in 2020, when job losses left more families short on groceries. Most are run by volunteers, who clean them, check dates and post rules, and local bakeries and grocers often donate unsold food. Organizers say the fridges succeed because they ask no questions; people who feel embarrassed to visit a food pantry can take what they need without signing a form. Keeping the fridges clean and stocked, however, depends on a steady supply of volunteers.

Student's summary: (1) Community fridges are public refrigerators where anyone can leave or take food at any time. (2) Volunteers keep them clean, and stores donate unsold food. (3) Their no-questions approach is the best way to fight hunger in America. (4) Their success depends on a steady supply of volunteers.

Which sentence should be removed from the student's summary?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
R.w: A summary must be objective and add nothing new. The passage reports that organizers credit the no-questions approach for the fridges' success; it never claims this is the best way to fight hunger nationwide. Sentence 3 adds the student's own judgment.

n.0: Sentence 1 accurately restates the opening definition, which a summary needs.
n.2: Sentence 2 condenses the key point about how the fridges are run and supplied.
n.3: Sentence 4 restates the passage's closing point about the fridges' reliance on volunteers.

R.q:
Read the passage.

By the time the ambulance reached Mercy Hospital, Elena had already called her brother twice. She had found their father on the kitchen floor that morning, awake but unable to lift his right arm. Earlier, at breakfast, he had complained that his coffee tasted strange and that his words felt "thick." Elena, a first-year nursing student, remembered a lecture from the week before about the warning signs of a stroke, and she dialed 911 before helping him sit up. Now, in the waiting room, she wished she had paid closer attention when he slurred his words at breakfast.

Place the events in the order in which they occurred, starting with the earliest.
o: Elena finds her father on the kitchen floor
Elena's father complains that his coffee tastes strange
Elena dials 911
Elena attends a lecture on the warning signs of a stroke
The ambulance reaches Mercy Hospital
R.w: The passage opens near the end and looks back. The lecture was "the week before." Breakfast came "earlier" than finding him on the floor. Elena dialed 911 after finding him (before helping him sit up). The ambulance's arrival at the hospital is the latest event described before the waiting-room scene.

R.q:
The HomeCheck 300 blood pressure monitor takes a reading in about 40 seconds and stores up to 120 results for two users. It runs on four AA batteries or the included wall adapter. The large, backlit screen is easy to read, and the cuff fits upper arms from 9 to 17 inches around. HomeCheck monitors have been sold in pharmacies since 2016. At $49.99, the HomeCheck 300 is a bargain, and customers will love how simple it is to use.

Which of the following statements from the product description are opinions? Select all that apply.
o: Customers will love how simple it is to use.
It runs on four AA batteries or the included wall adapter.
The cuff fits upper arms from 9 to 17 inches around.
HomeCheck monitors have been sold in pharmacies since 2016.
At $49.99, the HomeCheck 300 is a bargain.
The large, backlit screen is easy to read.
R.w: "Easy to read," "a bargain" and "customers will love" are judgments or predictions about feelings that buyers could dispute. The screen being large and backlit and the price being $49.99 are checkable, but each sentence's main claim is a judgment, so all three are opinions.

n.1: The power options can be checked by examining the product, so this is a fact.
n.2: The cuff range is a measurement that can be confirmed, so this is a fact.
n.3: Sales history can be confirmed through company or pharmacy records, so this is a fact.

R.q:
While studying for an anatomy quiz, Rosa comes across the word epistaxis in her textbook. The chapter uses the word several times but never shows how to say it. Tomorrow she will present a case study to her study group, and she wants to pronounce the word correctly and confirm whether it is a noun or a verb before she uses it.

Which source would best help Rosa?
o: The index of her textbook
An almanac of health statistics
A thesaurus of medical terms
A medical dictionary
R.w: A dictionary gives a word's pronunciation, part of speech, and definition, which is exactly what Rosa needs.

n.0: An index lists the pages where a term appears; it does not show pronunciation or part of speech.
n.1: An almanac compiles facts and figures, not word pronunciations.
n.2: A thesaurus lists words with similar meanings; it is not the place to find pronunciation.

R.q:
The Brookside Health Fair drew about 600 visitors to the community center on Saturday. Nurses from three local clinics offered free blood pressure checks, and a dentist handed out toothbrushes to children. Organizers called the event "our best fair yet" and plan to hold it again next spring. Sadly, the fair's single diabetes screening table could not keep up with the line. Dozens of people left without being tested, some after waiting more than an hour.

Which sentence from the passage most clearly reveals the author's perspective?
o: Nurses from three local clinics offered free blood pressure checks.
Organizers called the event "our best fair yet" and plan to hold it again next spring.
Dozens of people left without being tested, some after waiting more than an hour.
Sadly, the fair's single diabetes screening table could not keep up with the line.
R.w: "Sadly" is the author's own reaction, and it shows concern that the fair fell short in an important area. The other sentences report events or quote someone else without the author adding a judgment.

n.0: This neutrally reports a service that was offered.
n.1: "Our best fair yet" is a judgment, but it is the organizers' view, which the author quotes. A view the author reports is not the author's own perspective.
n.2: This sentence supports the author's concern, but it reports a checkable outcome without any judgment word; it does not state the author's attitude as clearly as "Sadly" does.

R.q:
The safety committee's report was succinct. In just two pages, it summarized six months of meetings, listed three recommendations and set a deadline for each. Board members, who were used to reports of fifty pages or more, praised the committee for its clarity and approved all three recommendations at the same meeting.

As used in the passage, the word succinct most nearly means
o: brief and to the point.
carefully and thoroughly researched.
easy to understand.
strongly worded.
R.w: "In just two pages" and the contrast with reports of "fifty pages or more" point to length. Succinct means brief and to the point.

n.1: Six months of meetings shows effort, but the clues next to succinct describe how short the report was, not how it was researched.
n.2: This matches a nearby word, "clarity," which describes a separate quality the board praised. The clues tied to succinct are about length.
n.3: Nothing describes the tone of the recommendations; the passage focuses on the report's length.

R.q:
While researching joint supplements for a health class, Marcus finds a polished website called JointHealthFacts. It features charts, quotations from customers, and a list of benefits of a glucosamine product called FlexWell, with a "Buy Now" button on every page. At the bottom of the home page, in small print, a line reads: "This site is owned and operated by FlexWell Nutrition, Inc." The site was updated two months ago.

What is the strongest reason to question this site's credibility?
o: It includes quotations from customers along with its scientific claims.
It is run by the company that profits from sales of the product it praises.
It was last updated two months ago rather than in the past few weeks.
It includes charts and numbers that may be hard for readers to follow.
R.w: The site's purpose is to sell FlexWell, and it is owned by the maker. That conflict of interest is the strongest reason to doubt that its information is balanced.

n.0: Customer quotations are weak evidence, but the deeper problem is who owns the site and why.
n.2: An update two months ago is reasonably current; the date is not the main problem.
n.3: Charts can be hard to read, but using data is not itself a reason to distrust a source.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Testing Your Well Water for Bacteria
1. Wash your hands. Do not touch the inside of the bottle or cap.
2. Remove the aerator (screen) from the end of the kitchen faucet.
3. Run cold water for 5 minutes.
4. Before filling, check that the white powder is still inside the bottle. Do not rinse it out.
5. Fill the bottle to the 100 mL line, not to the top.
6. Cap tightly and write the date and time of collection on the label.
7. Keep the sample cold and deliver it to the lab within 24 hours.

According to the directions, what should a person do immediately after running the cold water for 5 minutes?
o: Check that the white powder is still in the bottle
Remove the aerator from the end of the faucet
Fill the bottle with water up to the 100 mL line
Rinse the bottle out with the cold running water
R.w: Running the water is step 3. Step 4, checking that the powder is still in the bottle, comes next and must happen before filling.

n.1: Removing the aerator is step 2, which comes before running the water.
n.2: Filling is step 5; choosing it skips the powder check in step 4.
n.3: The directions say not to rinse the bottle, since that would remove the powder.

R.q:
Read the guidelines.

Volunteer Guidelines, Harbor Food Bank
Every new volunteer attends a one-hour orientation before working a first shift. After orientation, volunteers receive a login that lets them sign up for shifts online. Volunteers who wish to drive the delivery van must also show a valid driver's license to the warehouse manager and watch a twenty-minute road-safety video. Van drivers must be at least 21 years old. Shifts that involve lifting boxes heavier than 30 pounds are marked with a star on the online calendar.

Sam has just used his login to sign up online for a starred Saturday shift.

Based on the guidelines, which statement about Sam must be true?
o: Sam is at least 21 years old and has a valid driver's license.
Sam will drive the delivery van during Saturday's shift.
Sam has watched the twenty-minute road-safety video.
Sam has already completed the volunteer orientation.
R.w: Volunteers receive a login after orientation, and Sam used his login to sign up. So he must have completed orientation. The star tells us only that the shift involves heavy lifting.

n.0: The age and license rules apply to van drivers, and nothing says Sam is driving.
n.1: A starred shift means heavy lifting, not driving; nothing says Sam will drive.
n.2: The video is required for van drivers; Sam has signed up for a lifting shift.

R.q:
The research team had spent four months collecting blood samples from 200 volunteers. Then, during a power outage, the freezer that stored the samples failed overnight, and every sample was ruined. When the lead researcher, Dr. Kim, called the team together the next morning, she admitted that they were back to square one. Within a week, the team had begun recruiting new volunteers.

As used in the passage, the phrase "back to square one" means that the team was
o: returned to its original laboratory.
forced to start the work over.
waiting for the power to return.
blamed for losing the samples.
R.w: The idiom means having to start again from the beginning. The ruined samples and the team's decision to recruit new volunteers confirm that the work had to restart.

n.0: This reads the idiom literally as a place; the passage never mentions the team moving anywhere.
n.2: The outage had already happened; the idiom describes the loss of progress, not a wait for power.
n.3: No one is blamed; the freezer failed during a power outage.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Telehealth visits grew quickly when many clinics closed their waiting rooms in 2020. Patients who had never used video calls learned to meet their doctors through a phone screen, and many clinics kept offering the option after reopening.

Not every visit works well on a screen, however. A clinician cannot listen to a patient's lungs, feel a swollen joint, or draw blood through a video link. Patients without reliable internet or a private place to talk may struggle to take part. For these reasons, many clinics now use video for follow-up visits and medication checks while asking patients to come in person for new symptoms and physical exams.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the second paragraph?
o: Clinicians cannot examine joints, listen to lungs or draw blood over a video link.
Patients without reliable internet access are unable to take part in telehealth visits.
Telehealth grew rapidly in 2020 and remained common after clinics reopened their doors.
Video visits have limits, so clinics match in-person and video care to the type of visit.
R.w: The second paragraph opens with its topic sentence (not every visit works well on a screen), lists the limits, and ends with the result: clinics use video for some visits and in-person care for others. This option captures both the limits and the response.

n.0: Too narrow: these physical limits are supporting details for the paragraph's point, not the point itself.
n.1: Distortion of one detail: the passage says such patients may struggle, not that they are unable to take part.
n.2: Wrong part of the passage: this is the main idea of the first paragraph, not the second.

R.q:
Read the class schedule.

Community Center Fitness Classes, Fall Session
Class | Days | Time | Room
Chair Yoga | Mon, Wed | 9:00 to 9:45 a.m. | Studio A
Water Aerobics | Tue, Thu | 10:00 to 11:00 a.m. | Pool
Zumba | Mon, Thu | 6:00 to 7:00 p.m. | Gym
Strength Basics | Tue, Fri | 4:30 to 5:15 p.m. | Studio B
Tai Chi | Wed, Sat | 8:00 to 9:00 a.m. | Studio A
All classes are free for center members. Bring a water bottle and a towel.

Mr. Lee works Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. He wants a class whose two weekly meetings both fall outside his working hours. Based on the schedule, which class should he choose?
o: Strength Basics
Water Aerobics
Tai Chi
Zumba
R.w: Zumba meets Monday and Thursday from 6:00 to 7:00 p.m., after Mr. Lee's workday ends at 5 p.m., so both meetings fit.

n.0: Strength Basics starts at 4:30 p.m., before his workday ends at 5 p.m.
n.1: Water Aerobics meets on weekday mornings, during his work hours.
n.2: Tai Chi's Saturday meeting fits, but its Wednesday meeting at 8:00 a.m. falls during his work hours.

R.q:
Council member Reyes has proposed closing two blocks of Main Street to cars on Saturday mornings from May through September so that a farmers market can set up. Her opponent responded: "Reyes wants to ban cars from downtown. If she had her way, delivery trucks could not reach our stores, and shoppers who drive would have nowhere to go. I cannot support a plan that shuts down our business district."

Which statement best describes the flaw in the opponent's response?
o: It claims the plan is good or bad based on how many people favor it.
It attacks an exaggerated version of the plan instead of the real one.
It attacks Reyes's character instead of discussing her proposal.
It presents two choices as the only ones when others exist.
R.w: Reyes proposed closing two blocks on summer Saturday mornings, but the opponent describes a ban on cars downtown and argues against that. Misrepresenting a position to make it easier to attack is a straw man.

n.0: The response never mentions public opinion or popularity.
n.2: The opponent criticizes a (distorted) plan, not Reyes's character, so this is not ad hominem.
n.3: The response does not reduce the issue to two options; it rejects a misdescribed plan.

R.q:
(1) Mercy Valley Hospital should turn the empty lot behind its east wing into a community garden. Patients could see green space from their windows, staff could take breaks outdoors, and the hospital's nutrition program could teach classes using fresh vegetables.

(2) Some board members argue that the lot should be saved for a future parking garage. However, the hospital's own ten-year plan places new parking on the west side of campus, and a garden could be moved in a single season if plans ever changed.

(3) A garden would cost less than $20,000 to build. The board should approve it this spring.

What is the main purpose of paragraph 2?
o: to answer an objection to the author's proposal
to provide evidence that gardens improve patient health
to describe the location of the empty lot on the hospital campus
to summarize the costs and benefits of the garden
R.w: Paragraph 2 states an opposing view (save the lot for parking) and then rebuts it with the hospital's own plan and the garden's flexibility. Raising and answering an objection is a common purpose of a paragraph in a persuasive text.

n.1: Benefits to patients appear in paragraph 1, and no health evidence is offered anywhere in the passage.
n.2: The lot's location is given in paragraph 1; paragraph 2 mentions campus locations only to rebut the parking argument.
n.3: Cost appears only in paragraph 3, and paragraph 2 does not weigh costs against benefits.

R.q:
In January, trained observers on the fourth-floor medical unit at Bayview Hospital recorded staff cleaning their hands at 412 of 520 required moments, a rate of 79 percent. In late January, the unit installed alcohol gel dispensers beside every bed. The February audit found a rate of 91 percent. The report's author concluded, "The bedside dispensers were the best purchase the hospital made all year."

Which of the following best describes the author's conclusion?
o: It is a fact, because it is based on the measured hand-hygiene rates.
It is an opinion, because it relies on percentages that may be rounded.
It is a fact, because trained observers collected the data for the report.
It is an opinion, because it ranks this purchase above all others.
R.w: The audit rates are facts, but deciding that the dispensers were "the best purchase" of the year is a value judgment that goes beyond the data. Interpreting statistics in this way produces an opinion.

n.0: Facts can support a conclusion without making it a fact. "Best purchase" compares the dispensers to every other purchase, which the data do not measure and which people could judge differently.
n.1: The label is right but the reason is wrong. Rounded percentages are still checkable facts; the statement is an opinion because of the judgment word "best."
n.2: Who collected the data affects how reliable the rates are; it does not turn the author's judgment about the purchase into a fact.

R.q:
From a nurses' council proposal: Night-shift nurses on our medical units often skip their meal breaks to keep up with patient call lights. Fatigue and hunger make it harder to concentrate during the early morning medication pass. We propose that every night-shift nurse take a protected, uninterrupted 30-minute meal break, with a float nurse covering patients. We believe this change will reduce medication errors on night shift.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the proposal's argument?
o: Many nurses say that the meal break is the most welcome part of a long night shift.
On a unit that tested protected breaks, night-shift medication errors fell by a fifth.
Medication errors are reported more often on night shifts than on day shifts.
Night-shift nurses who take uninterrupted breaks will make fewer errors with medications.
R.w: A trial showing fewer night-shift errors after protected breaks were introduced is new evidence that links the proposed change to the predicted result.

n.0: Nurses' liking for breaks says nothing about medication errors.
n.2: This shows that night errors are a problem but not that protected breaks would reduce them.
n.3: This simply restates the proposal's conclusion; repeating a claim does not add support for it.

R.q:
Read the passage.

When our clinic switched to an online patient portal last spring, I expected to miss the phone calls. Instead, I found I could read my test results the day they came back, message my doctor at midnight without feeling like a bother, and refill a prescription in less time than it takes to brew coffee. My father, who is eighty-one, still prefers to call, and the clinic has kept a phone line for patients like him. I do wish the portal's menus were simpler; finding an old message can take five clicks. Those are small complaints, though, next to the hours I no longer spend on hold.

Which best describes the author's attitude toward the patient portal?
o: Reluctant acceptance of a change the author did not want
Mostly favorable, with a few minor reservations
Strong criticism of the portal's confusing menu design
Concern that the portal shuts out older patients
R.w: The author lists several benefits, mentions one complaint about the menus, and then calls it a "small complaint" compared with the time saved. That is a mostly positive attitude with minor reservations.

n.0: The author expected to miss phone calls, but the word "Instead" signals that the portal turned out better than expected.
n.2: Overstates the one complaint, which the author explicitly calls small.
n.3: The clinic kept a phone line for older patients like the author's father, so the author does not raise this concern.

R.q:
Westbrook Clinic offered walk-in flu shots this fall for the first time, in addition to scheduled appointments. The table shows the percentage of the clinic's patients in each age group who received a flu shot at the clinic.
Age group | Last year | This year
18 to 34 | 22% | 35%
35 to 64 | 41% | 47%
65 and older | 68% | 69%
The clinic manager plans to keep walk-in hours next year.

Which conclusions are supported by the passage and table? Select all that apply.
o: More patients aged 35 to 64 got a shot this year than patients aged 65 and older.
The youngest age group showed the largest increase in its vaccination rate.
Walk-in hours caused the rise in vaccination among patients aged 18 to 34.
Older patients used the walk-in hours more often than younger patients did.
Patients 65 and older had the highest vaccination rate of the three groups this year.
The percentage of patients who got a flu shot rose in each age group this year.
R.w: Every group rose (22 to 35, 41 to 47, 68 to 69). The 18 to 34 group gained 13 points, more than 6 or 1. At 69%, patients 65 and older had the highest rate this year.

n.0: The table gives percentages, not numbers of patients; without group sizes the counts cannot be compared.
n.2: Walk-in hours began the same year, but the table shows only rates, not why they changed; causation is not established.
n.3: The table does not separate walk-in shots from scheduled ones, so use of walk-in hours by age is unknown.

R.q:
To: Billing Department Staff
Subject: Forms (again)

As I have now explained at three separate meetings, completed insurance forms go in the blue tray, not the red one. I realize this may be a lot for some of you to keep track of, so I have taped a large, colorful sign above each tray with an arrow pointing to the right one. If anyone is still unsure, please feel free to stop by my office, and I will walk you through it slowly.

Which word best describes the tone of the memo?
o: lighthearted
accommodating
condescending
apologetic
R.w: Phrases such as "a lot for some of you to keep track of," the "large, colorful sign" and "walk you through it slowly" suggest the staff cannot handle a simple task. Talking down to the reader is a condescending tone.

n.0: The memo is not playful or trying to amuse; its mockery is aimed at the staff's abilities.
n.1: The offer of help looks accommodating on the surface, but "(again)," "three separate meetings" and "slowly" show irritation and talking down, not a genuine wish to help.
n.3: The writer apologizes for nothing; the memo places the blame on the staff.

R.q:
This year, Monroe Elementary began serving free breakfast in the cafeteria from 7:30 to 7:55 a.m. The principal reports that students who ate the school breakfast at least three times a week missed an average of 4 days of school, while students who did not eat it missed an average of 9 days. She concludes that the breakfast program improves attendance and plans to ask the district to expand it.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the principal's conclusion?
o: Students driven to school arrive in time for breakfast, but most bus riders arrive after it ends.
The breakfast program serves whole-grain cereal, low-fat milk, and fresh fruit to students each morning.
Teachers report that students who eat the school breakfast are less restless during morning classes.
Attendance improved most among the students who ate breakfast at school on every single school day.
R.w: If breakfast eaters are mostly students who are driven to school, a difference in families or transportation, rather than the breakfast, could explain the attendance gap. An alternative explanation weakens a causal conclusion.

n.1: The menu describes the program but does not affect whether it caused better attendance.
n.2: This supports a different benefit (behavior) and does not undercut the attendance claim.
n.3: More breakfast linked to more improvement is a dose pattern that supports the principal's conclusion.

R.q:
Opponents of the city's plan to put calorie counts on restaurant menus argue that diners do not read them and that the signs will only raise costs for small businesses. It is true that calorie labels alone will not solve obesity. But a 2018 study of a large restaurant chain found that customers ordered about 4 percent fewer calories after labels appeared, and many restaurants quietly made their dishes lighter. Those small changes add up across millions of meals. The council should pass the measure.

With which statement would the author most likely agree?
o: Calorie labels offer small benefits that add up over time.
Most diners do not read calorie counts printed on menus.
Calorie labels are not worth the cost to small businesses.
Calorie labels by themselves can solve the problem of obesity.
R.w: The author argues that a 4 percent reduction and lighter recipes "add up across millions of meals" and urges the council to pass the measure. Small but meaningful benefits sum up the author's view.

n.1: This is the opponents' claim, which the author reports in order to rebut it. A view the author reports is not necessarily the author's own.
n.2: This is also the opponents' argument; the author supports the measure despite the cost concern.
n.3: The author concedes that labels "alone will not solve obesity," so the author would reject this claim.

R.q:
Read the description of the line graph.

Title: Average Wait Time at Two Urgent Care Centers, by Time of Day
Legend: solid line = North Center; dashed line = South Center
Vertical axis: Average wait (minutes)
Plotted values (solid, dashed):
8 a.m.: 15, 25
10 a.m.: 20, 30
12 p.m.: 35, 30
2 p.m.: 40, 20
4 p.m.: 30, 15
6 p.m.: 25, 35
Values are averages for weekday visits during March.

A patient can visit either center at either 2 p.m. or 4 p.m. Based on the graph, which choice gives the shortest expected wait?
o: South Center at 4 p.m.
North Center at 4 p.m.
North Center at 2 p.m.
South Center at 2 p.m.
R.w: South Center is the dashed line. Its values are 20 minutes at 2 p.m. and 15 minutes at 4 p.m. North Center (solid) shows 40 and 30. The shortest of the four is South Center at 4 p.m., 15 minutes.

n.1: Swaps the legend: 15 minutes at 4 p.m. belongs to the dashed line (South); North's wait at 4 p.m. is 30 minutes.
n.2: North Center at 2 p.m. shows the longest wait of the four choices, 40 minutes.
n.3: South Center at 2 p.m. is 20 minutes, 5 minutes longer than at 4 p.m.

R.q:
We reached the trailhead at dawn, our breath fogging in the cold. By noon we had climbed above 11,000 feet, and my sister Leah said she felt dizzy and had a pounding headache. I remembered from our guidebook that altitude sickness often appears above 8,000 feet and that the safest treatment is to go back down. We turned around without reaching the summit. By the time we reached the lake at 9,500 feet, Leah's headache had eased, and we ate our sandwiches on a rock, watching the clouds drift over the peak we had left behind.

Which type of text is this passage?
o: narrative
technical
expository
persuasive
R.w: The passage tells a first-person story with characters, a setting and events in order (the climb, Leah's symptoms, the decision to turn back). That makes it a narrative.

n.1: No step-by-step instructions are given; the guidebook detail is remembered, not presented as directions.
n.2: The passage includes a fact about altitude sickness, but that fact is part of the story; the text as a whole recounts an experience rather than explaining a topic.
n.3: The narrator never argues for a position or urges the reader to act.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The Eastfield Library's summer reading challenge runs from June 10 to August 15. Readers of all ages may sign up at any branch or online. Children up to age 12 log minutes read; teens and adults log books finished. Every 300 minutes or every three books earns a ticket for the end-of-summer prize drawing, held August 22 at the main branch. Participants do not need to be present to win. Children who log 1,000 minutes also receive a free book of their choice, and teens who finish ten books earn a pass to the county pool. Last year, 2,140 people took part, up from 1,600 the year before.

Which of the following does the passage state? Select all that apply.
o: The prize drawing is held on August 22 at the main branch.
Teens and adults keep track of the number of books they finish.
Adults who finish ten books earn a pass to the county pool.
Participation grew by more than 1,000 people from the year before.
Prize winners must attend the drawing in order to collect a prize.
Children who log 1,000 minutes receive a free book of their choice.
R.w: The passage states that teens and adults log books finished, that children who log 1,000 minutes get a free book, and that the drawing is held August 22 at the main branch.

n.2: Wrong group: the pool pass is for teens who finish ten books, not adults.
n.3: Misreads the figures: participation rose from 1,600 to 2,140, an increase of 540 people.
n.4: Contradicted: participants do not need to be present to win.

R.q:
Passage 1
From the hospital newsletter: In this year's staff survey, 60 percent of our nurses said they would recommend Lakeside General as a place to work. That result reflects the strong teamwork and pride our nursing staff bring to every shift.

Passage 2
From a nurses' union bulletin: The same survey means that 40 percent of nurses would not recommend Lakeside as a workplace. With one in five nurses leaving each year, management should treat this number as a warning, not a reason to celebrate.

The authors disagree mainly about
o: whether nurse morale affects the quality of patient care
what the survey result shows about nurses' morale
whether the survey was conducted by the hospital itself
how many nurses said they would recommend the hospital
R.w: Both accept the same figure (60 percent would recommend, so 40 percent would not). The newsletter reads it as a sign of pride; the union reads it as a warning. They disagree about interpretation.

n.0: Neither passage discusses patient care.
n.2: Neither passage raises who conducted the survey.
n.3: Both use the same survey figures, so they agree about the numbers.

R.q:
Passage 1
Rural school districts struggle to hire teachers, who can often earn more in cities. A four-day school week offers something cities rarely can: a free weekday. It also saves districts money on buses and heating, though the main reason to adopt it is recruiting.

Passage 2
Two years after Pine Hollow District switched to a four-day week, student attendance had stayed about the same. Applications for open teaching jobs doubled. In a survey, many parents reported paying more for child care on the fifth day.

Which detail from Passage 2 best supports the main claim of Passage 1?
o: Student attendance stayed about the same after the switch.
Many parents reported higher child care costs on the fifth day.
Four-day weeks save districts money on buses and heating.
Applications for open teaching jobs doubled after the switch.
R.w: Passage 1's main claim is that a four-day week helps rural districts recruit teachers. Doubled teaching applications in Pine Hollow is direct evidence for that claim.

n.0: Stable attendance is a real finding, but it does not address teacher recruitment.
n.1: Higher child care costs are a drawback and do nothing to support the recruiting claim.
n.2: This detail comes from Passage 1, not Passage 2, and it is a side benefit rather than the main claim.

R.q:
Using Your Metered-Dose Inhaler

1. Remove the cap and shake the inhaler well for five seconds.
2. Breathe out fully, away from the inhaler.
3. Place the mouthpiece between your teeth and close your lips around it.
4. Press down on the canister once while breathing in slowly and deeply.
5. Hold your breath for 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly.
6. If a second puff is prescribed, wait one minute, shake the inhaler again and repeat steps 2 through 5.
7. If your inhaler contains a steroid, rinse your mouth with water after each use.

Which feature of this text most clearly marks it as technical writing rather than expository writing?
o: It numbers each action the reader must take, in order.
It uses a title that names the subject of the text.
It leaves out opinions and emotional language.
It presents accurate information about a medical device.
R.w: Technical (procedural) texts give exact, ordered directions for doing a task or using equipment. The numbered commands ("Remove," "Breathe out," "Hold your breath") set this text apart from an expository text, which explains a topic without walking the reader through actions step by step.

n.1: Expository articles also have titles naming their subject, so a title does not identify a text as technical.
n.2: Expository writing is also neutral and free of opinion, so this feature is shared by both types rather than distinguishing them.
n.3: Expository texts also present accurate information, so accuracy does not separate the two types.

R.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The human body has two kinds of sweat glands. Eccrine glands, found over most of the skin, release a watery sweat that cools the body as it evaporates. They are especially dense on the palms, the soles of the feet and the forehead.

(2) Apocrine glands are found mainly in the armpits and groin. They become active at puberty and release a thicker fluid containing proteins and fats. This fluid has no odor of its own; body odor develops when bacteria on the skin break it down.

(3) Both types are controlled by the nervous system, but they respond to different signals. Most eccrine glands respond mainly to heat, while apocrine glands respond mainly to emotional stress, which is why a nervous person may notice damp armpits even in a cool room.

According to paragraph 2, what causes body odor?
o: Watery eccrine sweat evaporating from the palms, soles and forehead
Emotional stress, which signals the apocrine glands to release their fluid
Proteins and fats in apocrine fluid, which have a strong odor of their own
Bacteria on the skin breaking down the fluid released by apocrine glands
R.w: Paragraph 2 states that apocrine fluid has no odor of its own and that body odor develops when bacteria on the skin break it down.

n.0: Wrong part of the passage: paragraph 1 describes eccrine sweat, which cools the body.
n.1: Wrong part of the passage: paragraph 3 says stress triggers apocrine glands to release fluid, which explains sweating, not odor.
n.2: Contradicts paragraph 2, which says the fluid has no odor of its own.

R.q:
To cut absences from stomach illness, Lincoln Elementary placed handwashing posters above every sink in October. The school nurse also taught a five-minute handwashing lesson in each classroom. From October through March, absences linked to stomach illness fell by 30 percent compared with the same months the year before. Absences at two nearby schools that made no changes stayed about the same. The custodians also reported that the soap dispensers needed refilling nearly twice as often as in past years.

The principal concludes that students washed their hands more often after the changes. Which detail best supports this conclusion?
o: The school nurse taught a five-minute handwashing lesson in each classroom.
Absences at two nearby schools that made no changes stayed about the same.
Absences linked to stomach illness fell by 30 percent from October through March.
Soap dispensers needed refilling nearly twice as often as in past years.
R.w: The conclusion is about a behavior: washing hands more often. Soap use nearly doubling is a direct measure of that behavior, so it gives the strongest support.

n.0: The lesson describes what the school did, not what students then did.
n.1: The comparison schools help rule out a seasonal explanation for fewer absences, but they say nothing about handwashing at Lincoln.
n.2: Fewer absences is an outcome that could have other causes; it supports the claim that illness fell, not that washing increased.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a beverage industry statement: A standard can of our energy drink contains about the same amount of caffeine as a large cup of coffee. Parents who are comfortable with their teenagers drinking coffee should have no greater concern about energy drinks.

Passage 2
From a pediatrician: A single can may hold about as much caffeine as coffee, but teenagers rarely sip energy drinks slowly the way they sip hot coffee. Many drink two or three cans quickly, often during sports, and some mix them with other caffeinated products. That pattern, not the single can, is what sends teens to emergency rooms with racing hearts.

How would the author of Passage 2 most likely respond to the claim in Passage 1?
o: The comparison ignores how quickly and in what amounts teens drink them.
Teens who drink coffee face the same risks as those who drink energy drinks.
Energy drinks contain much more caffeine per can than coffee does.
The industry is correct, so parents can set aside their concerns.
R.w: The pediatrician grants that one can is similar to coffee but argues that the real danger is drinking several cans quickly. That response targets the industry's single-can comparison.

n.1: The pediatrician contrasts how teens drink coffee and energy drinks, so the risks are not presented as the same.
n.2: The pediatrician concedes that a can may hold about as much caffeine as coffee.
n.3: The pediatrician describes emergency room visits, which shows continued concern.

R.q: Read the paragraph from a nursing program newsletter. Select the sentence that states the main idea of the paragraph.

parts.t: Last spring, a nursing student at Lakeview College fainted during an early clinical shift.
A review later found that she had skipped breakfast and slept only four hours the night before.
When the college surveyed its nursing students, nearly half said they often missed a meal before early shifts.
For nursing students, basic self-care is not a private matter, because it affects their safety and performance on clinical units.
The program now opens a breakfast cart at 6 a.m. and includes a session on sleep in its first-year orientation.

sn.a: Last spring, a nursing student at Lakeview College fainted during an early clinical shift.
sn.b: A review later found that she had skipped breakfast and slept only four hours the night before.
sn.c: When the college surveyed its nursing students, nearly half said they often missed a meal before early shifts.
sn.d: For nursing students, basic self-care is not a private matter, because it affects their safety and performance on clinical units.
sn.e: The program now opens a breakfast cart at 6 a.m. and includes a session on sleep in its first-year orientation.

R.w: Sentence 4 states the general point the rest of the paragraph builds toward: students' basic self-care affects their safety and performance on clinical units. The fainting episode, its causes and the survey are evidence for that point, and the breakfast cart and sleep session are the program's response to it.

n.a: The fainting episode is an opening anecdote that draws the reader in. It is one example, not the point the paragraph makes.
n.b: This explains why one student fainted. It supports the main idea but is too narrow to be it.
n.c: The survey result shows the problem is widespread. It is supporting evidence, not the conclusion the paragraph draws from that evidence.
n.e: The breakfast cart and sleep session are actions the program took in response to the main idea. They are specific details that follow from it, not the general point itself.

R.q:
Subject: Fire inspection moved to Tuesday
Hi everyone. The fire marshal's visit has moved up from Thursday to Tuesday at 9 a.m. Please have all hallways clear of linen carts and wheelchairs by the end of the Monday evening shift. At our last inspection, we were cited for two blocked exits on the third floor, and the marshal warned that a second citation would bring a fine. I will walk the third floor myself on Monday at 6 p.m. to check the exits. Thank you for your help.
Dana Ruiz, Facilities

Which conclusion is best supported by the email?
o: Dana is especially concerned about the condition of the third floor before Tuesday.
The inspection was moved up because Facilities asked the marshal for an earlier date.
Linen carts may be returned to the hallways once the marshal has left the building.
The fire marshal fined the facility for the two blocked exits on the third floor.
R.w: Dana mentions the earlier third-floor citation, the risk of a fine, and her plan to walk that floor personally on Monday. Together these show special concern about the third floor.

n.1: The email does not say why the date changed; the reason is not given.
n.2: The email says nothing about what happens after the inspection; this is an unsupported assumption.
n.3: The email says a second citation would bring a fine, which means the first citation did not.

R.q:
Read the email.

From: Priya Raman, Lab Coordinator
To: Nursing Cohort 2026
Subject: Change to Thursday's skills check-off
Sent: Tuesday, 3:14 p.m.

Hi everyone,
Because the simulation lab's air conditioning is being repaired, Thursday's IV skills check-off is moving from Lab 2 to Room 118 in the Allied Health building. The time is unchanged (1:00 to 4:00 p.m.), but please arrive 15 minutes before your assigned slot instead of 10. Bring your own gloves; the kits in Room 118 do not include them. If your slot is after 3:00, you may leave your bag in the student lounge next door.
Thanks, Priya

Darnell's assigned slot on Thursday is 2:30 p.m. According to the email, where and when should he arrive?
o: Room 118 at 2:15 p.m.
The student lounge at 2:15 p.m.
Room 118 at 2:20 p.m.
Lab 2 at 2:15 p.m.
R.w: The check-off has moved to Room 118, and students must now arrive 15 minutes before their slot: 2:30 minus 15 minutes is 2:15 p.m.

n.1: The lounge is for leaving bags, and only for students with slots after 3:00.
n.2: Uses the old 10-minute arrival rule, which the email replaces with 15 minutes.
n.3: Lab 2 is the old location; the check-off has moved to Room 118.

R.q:
Mercy General Hospital's volunteer program has grown to 160 members this year. Volunteers greet visitors, deliver flowers and mail, and push wheelchairs from the lobby to patient units. Everyone must complete eight hours of training before working a first shift. The youngest volunteer is 16 and the oldest is 87. According to the program's sign-up records, most volunteers are retired. Older volunteers, of course, struggle with the new tablet check-in system, so the hospital pairs them with high school volunteers. Many volunteers say the work gives them a sense of purpose.

Which sentence from the passage contains a stereotype?
o: Older volunteers, of course, struggle with the new tablet check-in system.
The youngest volunteer is 16 and the oldest is 87.
According to the program's sign-up records, most volunteers are retired.
Many volunteers say the work gives them a sense of purpose.
R.w: The sentence treats all older volunteers as struggling with technology, and "of course" presents that as obvious. An oversimplified generalization about a whole group is a stereotype.

n.1: Two ages are reported as facts. Mentioning age is not the same as making a generalization about an age group.
n.2: This reports a share taken from the program's own records, which can be checked. A statement about most members of a group that rests on records is a statistic, not an assumed trait applied to everyone in the group.
n.3: This reports what volunteers themselves said. "Many" describes a share of real responses, not an assumption about a group's traits.

R.q:
Passage 1
A 2023 study of six middle schools found that students threw away about a third of the food on their lunch trays. Fruit and vegetables were discarded most often. The waste costs districts money and sends tons of food to landfills each year.

Passage 2
This fall, Riverside Middle School placed a share table near the cafeteria exit. Students leave unopened milk, packaged snacks, and whole fruit they do not want, and classmates may take them. A local food pantry collects what is left each Friday. Food waste in the cafeteria fell by about 30 percent in three months.

Which statement best describes how Passage 2 relates to Passage 1?
o: It questions the data that Passage 1 uses to describe cafeteria waste.
It narrows Passage 1's topic to the cost of school lunches.
It repeats the main claim of Passage 1 using new statistics.
It describes one approach to the problem that Passage 1 explains.
R.w: Passage 1 describes the problem of cafeteria food waste. Passage 2 reports one school's share table and the 30 percent drop in waste that followed, which is a response to that problem.

n.0: Passage 2 never disputes Passage 1's findings; it assumes waste is a problem worth reducing.
n.1: Passage 2 does not discuss lunch costs; it describes a program that reduces waste.
n.2: Passage 2's statistic measures the result of a solution, not the size of the problem.

R.q:
A news article reports: "Only 31 percent of adults in Lane County got a flu shot last season." The county health department's online dashboard shows these figures for the same season.
Group | Got a flu shot
Adults 18 to 64 | 31%
Adults 65 and older | 67%
All adults 18 and older | 39%
The dashboard notes that its figures include shots given at clinics, pharmacies, and workplaces in the county.

Which statement best explains why the article's figure differs from the dashboard's figure for all adults?
o: The article's figure matches adults 18 to 64 and leaves out older adults.
The dashboard counts shots given in other counties, which raises its total.
The article rounded the dashboard's figure for all adults down to 31 percent.
The article used data from a different flu season than the dashboard did.
R.w: The article's 31 percent is exactly the dashboard's figure for adults 18 to 64. Leaving out adults 65 and older, who were vaccinated at 67 percent, gives a lower number than the 39 percent for all adults.

n.1: The dashboard says it counts shots given in the county; nothing suggests it includes other counties.
n.2: Rounding 39 cannot produce 31; the article's number matches a different group.
n.3: The passage says the dashboard shows figures for the same season as the article.

R.q:
Read the passage and the student's list.

At Valley Medical Center, a patient who arrives at the emergency department first stops at the triage desk, where a nurse checks vital signs and assigns a priority level. Next, a registration clerk records the patient's insurance and contact information. When a treatment room opens, the patient is moved there and examined by a physician or physician assistant. Any tests ordered, such as X-rays or blood work, are done next, and the patient waits for the results. Finally, the patient is either admitted to the hospital or discharged with instructions.

Student's list: triage; treatment room and exam; tests; admission or discharge.

Which step did the student leave out?
o: Discharge instructions given to the patient
Registration of insurance and contact information
Assignment of a priority level by the triage nurse
A follow-up visit with a specialist after discharge
R.w: The passage lists five steps: triage, registration, treatment room and exam, tests, and admission or discharge. The student's list skips registration, which comes between triage and the treatment room.

n.0: Discharge instructions are part of the final step, which the student included.
n.2: Assigning a priority level is part of triage, which the student included.
n.3: A follow-up visit is not part of the process the passage describes.

R.q:
Read the passage.

For years I believed I was simply bad at math. In high school I copied formulas onto index cards, memorized them the night before tests, and forgot them by the following week. When I enrolled in a nursing prerequisite course at twenty-eight, the instructor, Ms. Reyes, refused to hand out formulas to memorize. Instead she made us work out dosage problems with real medicine labels and explain each step aloud to a partner. The first month was miserable. By the final exam, though, I could set up a problem I had never seen before, and I realized I could not remember the last time I had written a formula on a card.

Which conclusion about the narrator is best supported by the passage?
o: The narrator's earlier struggles came from memorizing rather than understanding.
The narrator still prefers to memorize formulas on index cards before a test.
The narrator went on to earn the highest score in the prerequisite course.
The narrator found the course easy from the start because of Ms. Reyes's methods.
R.w: The narrator once memorized and quickly forgot formulas and believed they were bad at math. After learning to reason through problems and explain each step, the narrator could solve unfamiliar problems. The contrast suggests the earlier trouble came from the study method, not a lack of ability.

n.1: Opposite of the passage: the narrator no longer writes formulas on cards.
n.2: Unsupported: the passage says the narrator could solve new problems, not how the narrator ranked.
n.3: Contradicted: the narrator says the first month was miserable.

R.q:
Every evening, Mr. Okafor walked the length of his garden and studied the sky over the western ridge. The farmers in the valley joked that he trusted clouds more than the radio. That afternoon, the radio had promised a dry night. But as he finished his walk, he watched the swallows skim low over the field and felt the first cool gust that, in his experience, came about an hour before a storm. He stood still for a long moment, then turned toward the shed where he kept the canvas covers.

What will Mr. Okafor most likely do next?
o: Leave his plants uncovered because the radio predicted a dry night.
Ask the valley farmers whether they also expect a storm tonight.
Cover his plants because he expects a storm despite the forecast.
Harvest his ripest vegetables before a hard frost arrives tonight.
R.w: The passage says he trusts the sky over the radio, he notices the gust that usually comes before a storm, and he heads for the shed with the canvas covers. All point to covering his plants.

n.0: He turns toward the canvas covers, and he is known to trust the sky over the radio, so he is unlikely to rely on the forecast.
n.1: Nothing suggests he will consult anyone; he trusts his own reading of the sky and is already heading to the shed.
n.3: The signs he notices point to a storm; the passage mentions no cold or frost.

R.q:
Read the directions and the description.

Mixing Powdered Infant Formula
1. Wash your hands and clean the work area.
2. Boil fresh water, then let it cool for no more than 30 minutes.
3. Pour the water into a clean bottle first, then add the powder.
4. Use the scoop from the can and level each scoop with a clean knife. Add one level scoop for every 2 fluid ounces of water.
5. Cap the bottle and shake until the powder dissolves.
6. Cool the bottle under running water, and test a few drops on your inner wrist before feeding.

After washing his hands and wiping the counter, Terrell boiled fresh water and let it cool for 20 minutes. He put three heaping scoops of powder into a clean bottle, poured in 6 fluid ounces of the water, and shook the bottle until the powder dissolved. He cooled the bottle under running water and tested a few drops on his wrist.

Which directions did Terrell fail to follow? Select all that apply.
o: Use one scoop of powder for every 2 fluid ounces of water
Test a few drops on the inner wrist before feeding
Pour the water into the bottle before adding the powder
Level each scoop of powder with a clean knife
Let the boiled water cool for no more than 30 minutes
R.w: Terrell put the powder in before the water (step 3 says water first) and used heaping scoops instead of level ones (step 4). He followed the other directions.

n.0: Three scoops for 6 fluid ounces is the correct ratio of one scoop per 2 ounces; the error was that the scoops were heaping.
n.1: He tested a few drops on his wrist, as directed.
n.4: He let the water cool for 20 minutes, within the 30-minute limit.

M.q: A sports drink mix calls for 12 scoops of powder for every 18 cups of water. Which mixtures have the same ratio of scoops to cups? Select all that apply.
o: 8 scoops per 12 cups
14 scoops per 20 cups
30 scoops per 45 cups
3 scoops per 2 cups
6 scoops per 12 cups
2 scoops per 3 cups
M.w: 12:18 simplifies to 2:3 (divide both terms by 6). 8:12 = 2:3 (divide by 4) and 30:45 = 2:3 (divide by 15), so all three match.

n.1: This adds 2 to each term. Equivalent ratios multiply or divide both terms by the same number; 14:20 = 7:10, not 2:3.
n.3: 3:2 reverses the order of the ratio; it has more powder than water.
n.4: This halves the scoops but not the cups. 6:12 = 1:2, a weaker mix than 2:3.

M.q: A table shows the volume remaining in a patient's IV bag: 0 minutes, 1,000 mL; 30 minutes, 940 mL; 60 minutes, 880 mL; 90 minutes, 820 mL. If this constant rate continues, how many minutes after the start will the bag hold 400 mL?

tr.200: 400 / 2, the time to empty the last 400 mL
tr.210: the time after the 90-minute reading (420 / 2), not after the start
tr.500: 1,000 / 2, the time to empty the full bag

M.w: Rate of change = (940 - 1,000) / 30 = -2 mL per minute. To fall from 1,000 to 400 mL is 600 mL, which takes 600 / 2 = 300 minutes.

M.q: A home health nurse drives 24 miles at an average of 32 miles per hour to reach her first patient, then 35 miles at 60 miles per hour to reach her second. What is her total driving time?
o: 1 h 33 min
1 h 17 min
1 h 20 min
45 min
M.w: Time = distance ÷ speed. Leg 1: 24 ÷ 32 = 0.75 h = 45 min. Leg 2: 35 ÷ 60 = 7/12 h = 35 min. Total: 45 + 35 = 80 min = 1 h 20 min.

n.0: 1 h 33 min reads 1.33 hours as 1 hour 33 minutes; 0.33 h is about 20 minutes.
n.1: 1 h 17 min divides the total distance by the average of the two speeds (59 ÷ 46); the legs must be timed separately.
n.3: 45 min is the time for the first leg only.

M.q: A child weighs 44 pounds. The provider orders one dose of a medication at 10 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. The oral suspension contains 40 milligrams in every 5 milliliters. Use 1 kilogram = 2.2 pounds. How many milliliters make up one dose?
o: 5 mL
55 mL
25 mL
121 mL

n.0: 200 ÷ 40 = 5 is the number of 5 mL portions in the dose; multiply by 5 mL to get 25 mL.
n.1: This uses the weight in pounds without converting to kilograms (44 × 10 = 440 mg; 440 ÷ 40 × 5 = 55 mL).
n.3: This multiplies 44 by 2.2 (96.8 kg) instead of dividing, which gives 968 mg and 121 mL.

M.q: Solve for x: 5(x - 2) = 3(x + 4).
M.w: Distribute: 5x - 10 = 3x + 12. Subtract 3x: 2x - 10 = 12. Add 10: 2x = 22. Divide by 2: x = 11. Check: 5(9) = 45 and 3(15) = 45.

n.0: Sign error when moving -10: the right side becomes 12 + 10 = 22, not 12 - 10 = 2.
n.1: This adds 3x to the left side instead of subtracting it, giving 8x - 10 = 12, so 8x = 22.
n.2: This distributes to the x terms only, giving 5x - 2 = 3x + 4, so 2x = 6.

M.q: A child's liquid antibiotic dose is 1 1/2 teaspoons twice a day. The bottle holds 4 fluid ounces. Use 1 fluid ounce = 30 milliliters. How many full days will the bottle last at this dose?
o: 8 days
16 days
4 days
2 days
M.w: Dose = 1.5 × 5 mL = 7.5 mL; per day = 2 × 7.5 = 15 mL. Bottle = 4 × 30 = 120 mL. 120 ÷ 15 = 8 days.

n.1: This counts one dose per day (120 ÷ 7.5); the dose is given twice a day.
n.2: This uses 15 mL per fluid ounce; the stem gives 1 fl oz = 30 mL.
n.3: This uses 15 mL per teaspoon, which is the tablespoon amount; 1 tsp = 5 mL.

M.q: Four tables each list three (x, y) pairs. In which table does y vary directly with x?
M.w: Direct variation needs the same ratio y / x for every pair: 6 / 4 = 1.5, 9 / 6 = 1.5, 15 / 10 = 1.5. So y = 1.5x.

n.0: Each product xy is 36, which is inverse variation.
n.1: The ratio is 1.5 for the first two pairs but 9 / 8 = 1.125 for the third.
n.2: y rises 2 per unit of x, but y = 2x + 5 has a starting value of 5, so the ratios (7, 4.5, 3.25) differ.

M.q: A trend line relating certified nursing assistants' years of experience (x) to hourly wage in dollars (y) is y = 0.75x + 16.50. What does the 0.75 represent?
o: The predicted wage increase for each additional year
The predicted number of years needed to earn $16.50
The predicted hourly wage after one year of experience
The predicted starting wage for a CNA with no experience
M.w: In y = mx + b, the slope m is the change in y for each 1-unit increase in x. Here wages are predicted to rise $0.75 per hour for each additional year.

n.1: $16.50 is predicted at 0 years; 0.75 is a rate, not a number of years.
n.2: After one year the predicted wage is 0.75 + 16.50 = $17.25, not $0.75.
n.3: The starting wage (x = 0) is the y-intercept, $16.50.

M.q: A bottle contains 15 tablets. Each prescribed dose is 3/4 of a tablet, and tablets are scored so they can be split. How many doses does the bottle contain?
M.w: Divide the supply by the dose: 15 ÷ 3/4 = 15 × 4/3 = 60/3 = 20 doses.

n.0: 11 1/4 is 15 × 3/4, the multiplication instead of the division.
n.2: 5 divides 15 by the numerator 3 and ignores the denominator 4.
n.3: 60 multiplies by 4 but does not then divide by 3.

M.q: A line graph shows the number of registered nurses employed in a county: 2000, 12,000; 2005, 13,500; 2015, 15,500; 2020, 16,800. The years on the horizontal axis are plotted to scale. During which interval was the average increase per year the greatest?
M.w: Divide each change by the number of years. 2000 to 2005: 1,500 / 5 = 300 per year. 2005 to 2015: 2,000 / 10 = 200 per year. 2015 to 2020: 1,300 / 5 = 260 per year. 2005 to 2020: 3,300 / 15 = 220 per year. The greatest is 2000 to 2005.

n.1: This interval has the largest total increase (2,000), but it covers 10 years, so it averages 200 per year.
n.2: 1,300 over 5 years is 260 per year, less than the 300 per year from 2000 to 2005.
n.3: 3,300 over 15 years averages 220 per year.

M.q: Of the 640 students in a prerequisite course, 45% are taking the TEAS this semester, and 75% of those students plan to apply to a BSN program. How many students in the course plan to apply?
M.w: Taking the TEAS: 0.45 × 640 = 288. Planning to apply: 0.75 × 288 = 216. (Equivalently, 0.45 × 0.75 = 0.3375 and 0.3375 × 640 = 216.)

n.1: This takes 75% of all 640 students instead of 75% of the 288 taking the TEAS.
n.2: This subtracts the percents (75% - 45% = 30%) and takes 30% of 640. A percent of a percent is found by multiplying.
n.3: This is the number taking the TEAS; 75% of those 288 students still has to be found.

M.q: In a pictograph of blood donations, each full blood-drop icon represents 12 units and each half icon represents 6 units. The rows show Monday 4 1/2 icons, Tuesday 3 icons, Wednesday 6 icons, and Thursday 2 1/2 icons. How many units of blood were donated over the four days?

n.0: 16 is the number of icons, not the number of units they represent.
n.1: 204 = 17 x 12 counts each half icon as a full icon.
n.3: 180 = 15 x 12 drops both half icons.

M.q: A clinic recorded how many doses of a medicine each of 33 patients missed in one month. The bar graph shows how many patients missed each number of doses. Select the bar that represents the median number of missed doses.
M.w: With 33 patients listed in order, the median is the 17th value. Patients 1 to 12 missed 0 doses and patients 13 to 21 missed 1 dose, so the 17th patient, and the median, is 1 missed dose.

n.a: 0 is the mode, the value with the most patients (the tallest bar). It covers only patients 1 to 12, so it does not reach the 17th patient.
n.c: 2 is the middle label on the axis, but the median depends on how many patients are in each bar. 2 doses covers patients 22 to 27.
n.d: 3 doses covers patients 28 to 31, well above the middle.
n.e: 4 doses covers patients 32 and 33, the two highest values.

M.q: The mean price of 10 homes sold on a street last year was $310,000. If the one home that sold for $940,000 is removed, what is the mean price of the other 9 homes, in thousands of dollars? Enter the number only.

tr.310: the original mean, before the outlier is removed

M.w: Total of 10 homes = 10 x 310 = 3,100 thousand. Remove 940: 3,100 - 940 = 2,160 thousand. Mean of 9 = 2,160 / 9 = 240 thousand dollars.

M.q: An L-shaped room is formed from a 20-foot by 12-foot rectangle with a 6-foot by 5-foot closet cut out of one corner. The closet is not part of the room. What is the floor area of the L-shaped room?
o: 270 ft²
64 ft²
240 ft²
210 ft²
M.w: Full rectangle = 20 × 12 = 240 ft². Closet = 6 × 5 = 30 ft². Room = 240 - 30 = 210 ft².

n.0: This adds the closet area (30 ft²) instead of subtracting it.
n.1: 64 ft is the perimeter of the L-shaped room, not its area.
n.2: This is the full rectangle; the 30 ft² closet must be subtracted.

M.q: A county's sales tax rate is stored in a spreadsheet as the decimal 0.0375. What is this tax rate written as a percent? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.0.375: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.37.5: Moved the decimal point 3 places right.

M.w: To change a decimal to a percent, multiply by 100 (move the decimal point 2 places right): 0.0375 × 100 = 3.75, so the rate is 3.75%.

M.q: The table shows how students in three grades usually get to school. Select the cell for the group that makes up exactly 25 percent of all Grade 10 students.
M.w: Grade 10 total = 30 + 54 + 36 = 120. 25% of 120 = 0.25 x 120 = 30, and the Grade 10 group with 30 students is the walkers.

n.w9: 20 is a Grade 9 count (20% of the 100 Grade 9 students), not a Grade 10 group.
n.w11: 25 Grade 11 walkers are 25% of Grade 11 (25 + 40 + 35 = 100), but the question asks about Grade 10.
n.b9: 50 is a Grade 9 count, half of Grade 9.
n.b11: 40 is a Grade 11 count, 40% of Grade 11.
n.c9: This cell also shows 30, the target number, but these are Grade 9 car riders (30% of Grade 9), not Grade 10 students.
n.c11: 35 is a Grade 11 count, 35% of Grade 11.

M.q: A nursing program needs lab coats for 150 students and 8 instructors. It already has 10 new coats in storage, and more coats come only in boxes of 12. What is the least number of boxes the program must order so that everyone gets a coat?
o: 12 boxes
11 boxes
13 boxes
14 boxes
M.w: Coats needed: 150 + 8 = 158. Subtract the 10 in storage: 158 - 10 = 148. Boxes: 148 ÷ 12 = 12.33. Twelve boxes hold only 144 coats, so round up to 13 boxes (156 coats, enough for the 148 still needed).

n.0: 12 boxes rounds 12.33 down; 12 boxes plus storage give 144 + 10 = 154 coats, 4 short.
n.1: 11 boxes subtracts the 8 instructors instead of adding them (150 - 8 - 10 = 132, and 132 ÷ 12 = 11).
n.3: 14 boxes ignores the 10 coats in storage (158 ÷ 12 = 13.17, rounded up), so it orders one box too many.

M.q: A pharmacy sells the same brand of vitamin gummies in four bottle sizes. Which bottle has the lowest price per gummy?
o: 24 gummies for $5.04
40 gummies for $8.20
16 gummies for $3.52
32 gummies for $6.08
M.w: Unit price = price ÷ quantity. $6.08 ÷ 32 = $0.19 per gummy, the lowest of $0.21, $0.19, $0.205, and $0.22.

n.0: $5.04 ÷ 24 = $0.21 per gummy, which is more than $0.19.
n.1: This is the largest bottle, but $8.20 ÷ 40 = $0.205 per gummy, which is more than $0.19.
n.2: This has the lowest total price, but $3.52 ÷ 16 = $0.22 per gummy, the highest unit price.

M.q: A rectangular storage bin in a hospital supply room is 2.5 feet long, 2 feet wide, and 1.5 feet tall. How many cubic feet of supplies can the bin hold when it is filled to the top?
o: 6 ft³
7.5 ft³
23.5 ft³
3.75 ft³

n.0: This adds the three dimensions; volume multiplies them.
n.2: 23.5 is the surface area of the bin in square feet, 2(5 + 3.75 + 3), not its volume.
n.3: This multiplies the length by the height (2.5 × 1.5) but leaves out the width.

M.q: Destiny invested $5,000, part in an account paying 6% simple annual interest and the rest in an account paying 4%. After one year she earned $260 in interest in total. How many dollars did she invest in the 6% account? Enter the amount in dollars.

tr.1000: Dropped the -x, treating all $5,000 as earning 4% and giving 0.06x = 60.
tr.2000: Found the amount in the 4% account instead of the 6% account.

M.q: A survey at a health fair found that 7 of every 20 visitors had their blood pressure checked. If 1,260 people visited the fair, how many would be expected to have had their blood pressure checked?
M.w: Set up 7/20 = x/1,260. Cross-multiply: 20x = 8,820, so x = 441.

n.0: This divides 1,260 by 7 instead of multiplying by 7/20.
n.1: This is 1/20 of the visitors, the size of one part, not 7 parts.
n.2: This is the number expected not to have had a check (13 of every 20).

M.q: A health survey reports that 22.5% of adults in a county walk to work at least once a week. Which fraction, in lowest terms, is equivalent to 22.5%?

n.0: 1/4 = 25%. It rounds 22.5% to 25% before converting, which changes the value.
n.2: 9/400 = 0.0225, which is 2.25%. The decimal point was moved one place too far.
n.3: 9/4 = 2.25. This writes the percent over 10 instead of 100.

M.q: The daily low temperatures in Duluth over five winter days were -6°F, 3°F, -2°F, -9°F and 4°F. What was the mean daily low temperature?
M.w: Sum: -6 + 3 + (-2) + (-9) + 4 = -10. Divide by the number of days: -10 ÷ 5 = -2°F.

n.0: 2°F drops the negative sign of the sum -10.
n.1: 4.8°F adds the absolute values (6 + 3 + 2 + 9 + 4 = 24) and ignores the negative signs.
n.3: -2.5°F divides the sum by 4 instead of by the 5 days.

M.q: A wheelchair wheel has a radius of 14 inches. How far does the wheelchair travel when the wheel makes one complete turn without slipping? Use 3.14 for pi.
M.w: One turn moves the chair one circumference. C = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 14 = 87.92 in.

n.0: This finds the area (πr²) instead of the circumference.
n.1: This multiplies pi by the radius; circumference is 2πr.
n.2: This multiplies 2π by the diameter (28 in); use C = 2πr or C = πd.

M.q: Four students each completed part of the same online module. The parts completed were 5/9, 4/7, 6/11 and 7/13. Which fraction of the module is greatest?
M.w: Convert to decimals: 4/7 ≈ 0.571, 5/9 ≈ 0.556, 6/11 ≈ 0.545, 7/13 ≈ 0.538. The greatest is 4/7. (Cross-multiplying 4/7 and 5/9 also works: 4 × 9 = 36 > 5 × 7 = 35.)

n.0: 5/9 ≈ 0.556, slightly less than 4/7 ≈ 0.571 (cross products 35 < 36).
n.1: 7/13 ≈ 0.538 is actually the least; a larger denominator does not mean a larger fraction.
n.2: 6/11 ≈ 0.545; its larger numerator and denominator do not make it larger.

M.q: Lin buys 3 scrub tops at $24.50 each and 2 pairs of scrub pants at $19.75 each. She uses a coupon for $10 off her total purchase and pays with $150. How much change should she receive? Enter the amount in dollars.

tr.27: Added the $10 coupon to the cost instead of subtracting it.
tr.103: Gave the amount paid after the coupon instead of the change.

M.q: On a state map, 1.5 inches represents 40 miles. Two towns are 5.25 inches apart on the map. What is the actual distance between the two towns?
o: 141.75 miles
210 miles
315 miles
140 miles
M.w: Set up 1.5/40 = 5.25/d. Cross-multiply: 1.5d = 210, so d = 140 miles.

n.0: This rounds 26.67 miles per inch to 27 before multiplying. Round only at the end.
n.1: This multiplies 5.25 by 40 as if 1 inch represented 40 miles.
n.2: This multiplies 40 by 1.5 to get 60 miles per inch instead of dividing.

M.q: Each of the 15 employees at a pharmacy receives a raise of $2.00 per hour. Before the raise, the hourly wages had a mean of $18.40, a median of $17.75, and a range of $9.50. Which describes the wages after the raise?
o: Mean $20.40, median $19.75, range $11.50
Mean $20.40, median $19.75, range $9.50
Mean $18.53, median $19.75, range $9.50
Mean $20.40, median $17.75, range $9.50
M.w: Adding the same amount to every value adds it to the mean and the median, but the gap between the highest and lowest wage does not change. Mean 18.40 + 2 = 20.40; median 17.75 + 2 = 19.75; range stays 9.50.

n.0: The range does not change: the highest and lowest wages both rise by $2.
n.2: Each employee gets $2, so the mean rises by $2, not by 2 / 15.
n.3: The middle wage also rises by $2, so the median becomes $19.75.

M.q: A lab balance displays the mass of a sample as 47.0652 grams. The lab report requires masses rounded to the nearest hundredth of a gram. What mass should be reported?
M.w: The hundredths digit is 6. The digit to its right (thousandths) is 5, so round up: 47.0652 → 47.07 g.

n.0: 47.065 g rounds to the nearest thousandth.
n.2: 47.1 g rounds to the nearest tenth, not the nearest hundredth.
n.3: 47.06 g truncates; the next digit is 5, so the hundredths digit rounds up.

M.q: A nursing student must complete at least 120 clinical hours. She has already completed 47.5 hours, and each clinical shift is 7.5 hours long. What is the least number of additional shifts she must complete?
M.w: Write 47.5 + 7.5s ≥ 120. Subtract 47.5: 7.5s ≥ 72.5. Divide by 7.5: s ≥ 9.67. Shifts are whole, so she needs at least 10 (47.5 + 75 = 122.5 hours).

n.0: This rounds 9.67 down. Nine shifts give 47.5 + 67.5 = 115 hours, which is short of 120.
n.1: This divides the full 120 hours by 7.5 and ignores the 47.5 hours already completed.
n.3: Sign error: this adds 47.5 to 120 instead of subtracting it, giving 167.5 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 22.3, then rounds up.

M.q: A patient's oral intake record for one day shows: 8 a.m. water 240 mL, 10 a.m. juice 180 mL, noon soup 360 mL, 3 p.m. tea 120 mL, 6 p.m. milk 300 mL. What percent of the day's total intake was taken before noon? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.420: the milliliters before noon, not the percent

M.q: A patient in a cardiac rehabilitation program walks 1 mile in 16 minutes at a steady pace. What is the patient's walking speed in feet per second?
o: 330 ft/s
5.5 ft/s

n.0: 330 is the speed in feet per minute (5,280 ÷ 16); divide by 60 to get feet per second.
n.1: This divides seconds by feet (960 ÷ 5,280), which gives seconds per foot.
n.3: 3.75 is the speed in miles per hour (60 ÷ 16), not feet per second.

M.q: The wait times, in minutes, for seven patients at an urgent care center were 12, 14, 14, 16, 17, 18, and 65. Which measure best describes a typical wait time for these patients, and why?
o: The mean, because it uses every value in the data set
The median, because the 65-minute wait pulls the mean up
The range, because it shows the spread from 12 to 65
The mode, because 14 is the most common wait time
M.w: The mean is 156 / 7 = 22.3 minutes, higher than six of the seven waits because the outlier 65 pulls it up. The median, 16, is resistant to the outlier and describes a typical wait.

n.0: Using every value is exactly why the mean is distorted here: the 65 drags it above six of the seven waits.
n.2: The range measures spread, not a typical value, and it is inflated by the outlier.
n.3: 14 appears only twice in seven values, so it says little about the center.

M.q: The roof truss of a house is an isosceles triangle. The angle at the peak, between the two equal sloping sides, measures 112°. What is the measure of each of the two base angles of the truss?
M.w: In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal. (180 - 112) ÷ 2 = 68 ÷ 2 = 34°.

n.0: This uses 360°, the angle sum of a quadrilateral, instead of 180°.
n.1: 68° is both base angles together (180 - 112); divide by 2.
n.3: This halves the peak angle; the base angles share what is left of 180°.

M.q: On a number line, point Q is located exactly halfway between -1/2 and 3/4. What is the value of point Q?
M.w: The midpoint is the average: (-1/2 + 3/4) ÷ 2 = (-2/4 + 3/4) ÷ 2 = 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8. Check: from -1/2 up 5/8 gives 1/8, and from 1/8 up 5/8 gives 3/4.

n.0: 1/4 is the sum -1/2 + 3/4; it still needs to be divided by 2.
n.2: 5/8 is half of the distance between the points (1 1/4 ÷ 2), not the location of the midpoint.
n.3: -1/8 has the wrong sign; -2/4 + 3/4 is positive.
