M.q: Which values of x satisfy the inequality 2(x - 3) < 5x + 9? Select all that apply.
M.w: Distribute: 2x - 6 < 5x + 9. Subtract 5x: -3x - 6 < 9. Add 6: -3x < 15. Divide by -3 and reverse the sign: x > -5. So -4.5, 0, and 3 work. Check -4.5: 2(-7.5) = -15 and 5(-4.5) + 9 = -13.5; -15 < -13.5 is true.

n.2: -7 is less than -5. Check: 2(-10) = -20 and 5(-7) + 9 = -26; -20 < -26 is false.
n.3: At x = -5 both sides equal -16, and -16 < -16 is false because the inequality is strict.
n.4: -6 is less than -5. Check: 2(-9) = -18 and 5(-6) + 9 = -21; -18 < -21 is false. Choosing it comes from keeping the sign (x < -5).

M.q: This fall a pharmacy gave 135% of the number of flu vaccines it gave last fall. Last fall it gave 1,200 vaccines. How many flu vaccines did it give this fall?

n.0: This is 35% of 1,200, the increase alone, not 135% of 1,200.
n.3: This adds 135% of 1,200 to the original 1,200, counting last fall's vaccines twice.

S.q: A student is reviewing a data table and must flag every value that contains exactly three significant figures. Which values should be flagged? Select all that apply.
S.w: 0.00250 has 3 (leading zeros do not count; the trailing zero after the decimal does). 2.50 has 3 (trailing zero after a decimal point counts). 205 has 3 (a zero between nonzero digits counts).

n.0: 0.025 has 2 significant figures; the leading zeros are placeholders.
n.2: 0.002500 g has 4 significant figures: the 2, the 5 and both trailing zeros after the decimal point.
n.4: With no decimal point, the trailing zero in 250 is not counted as significant, giving 2 significant figures.

S.q: A nutrition student is classifying carbohydrates found in foods and in the body. Which of these are polysaccharides? Select all that apply.
o: Glycogen
Starch
Lactose
Cellulose
Sucrose
Glucose
S.w: Starch (plant storage), glycogen (animal storage) and cellulose (plant cell walls) are polysaccharides, long chains of glucose units.

n.2: Lactose is a disaccharide (glucose + galactose).
n.5: Glucose is a monosaccharide, the monomer of these polysaccharides.

S.q: After a long course of a broad-spectrum antibiotic, a patient develops severe diarrhea caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile in the colon. Which explanation is most likely?
o: The antibiotic converted harmless gut bacteria into C. difficile.
The antibiotic killed normal gut bacteria that kept C. difficile in check.
The antibiotic caused the patient's own colon cells to divide rapidly.
The antibiotic weakened the colon wall, letting viruses enter.
S.w: Normal microbiota compete with pathogens. Killing them with an antibiotic lets an opportunistic pathogen such as C. difficile overgrow.

n.0: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria; they do not turn one bacterial species into another.
n.2: The diarrhea is caused by an overgrowing pathogen, not by the patient's own cells dividing.
n.3: C. difficile is a bacterium, and the disease here is bacterial overgrowth, not viral entry.

S.q: A student runs a reaction twice with the same reactant amounts and temperature, adding a catalyst the second time. Which outcome should the student predict for the second run?
o: A faster reaction that forms the same products
A faster reaction that forms different products
A faster reaction that uses up the catalyst
A slower reaction that forms different products
S.w: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the reaction goes faster. It is not consumed and does not change which products form.

n.1: The rate rises, but the products are unchanged; a catalyst does not alter the reaction's outcome.
n.2: A catalyst is regenerated at the end of the reaction; it is not used up as a reactant.
n.3: A catalyst speeds a reaction, and the products stay the same.

S.q: Which of the following give a person passive immunity? Select all that apply.
o: Maternal IgG crossing the placenta to a fetus
Recovery from a natural chickenpox infection
An injection of tetanus immune globulin after a wound
IgA received by an infant through breast milk
An mRNA vaccine against a respiratory virus
A tetanus toxoid vaccine given as a booster
S.w: Passive immunity means receiving ready-made antibodies: naturally (IgG across the placenta, IgA in breast milk) or artificially (immune globulin, antivenom, antitoxin). Vaccines and infections make the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells, which is active immunity.

n.1: Having the infection gives naturally acquired active immunity.
n.4: Vaccines, including mRNA vaccines, give artificially acquired active immunity.
n.5: A toxoid vaccine stimulates the body to make its own antibodies and memory cells: artificially acquired active immunity.

S.q: Which enzyme is correctly matched with both the site where it acts and the nutrient it digests?
o: Pancreatic lipase: small intestine; starch
Salivary amylase: small intestine; starch
Pepsin: stomach; proteins
Trypsin: stomach; proteins
S.w: Pepsin acts in the stomach on proteins. Each other option gets either the site or the nutrient wrong.

n.0: Pancreatic lipase does act in the small intestine, but it digests fats, not starch.
n.1: Salivary amylase digests starch, but it acts in the mouth; pancreatic amylase digests starch in the small intestine.
n.3: Trypsin digests proteins, but it acts in the small intestine, where pancreatic juice enters, not in the stomach.

S.q: A lab has 4.8 × 10⁹ bacteria to spread evenly across 1.2 × 10³ agar plates. How many bacteria go on each plate?
S.w: To divide in scientific notation, divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents: (4.8 / 1.2) × 10⁽⁹⁻³⁾ = 4.0 × 10⁶ bacteria per plate.

n.0: This subtracts the coefficients (4.8 - 1.2) instead of dividing them.
n.2: This adds the exponents (9 + 3), the rule for multiplication; division subtracts them.
n.3: This divides the exponents (9 / 3) instead of subtracting them.

S.q: A histology student is comparing the four basic tissue types. Which feature distinguishes connective tissue from epithelial, muscle and nervous tissue?
o: Cells that generate and conduct electrical impulses
Cells scattered within an extracellular matrix of fibers
Cells joined tightly together with an exposed free surface
Cells that shorten when stimulated to produce movement
S.w: Connective tissue cells are scattered within an extracellular matrix made of ground substance and fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular). In blood, the matrix is fluid plasma.

n.0: Generating and conducting impulses describes the neurons of nervous tissue.
n.2: Tightly joined cells with a free (apical) surface describe epithelial tissue.
n.3: Contractility describes muscle tissue.

S.q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is described as a strong acid, while the acetic acid in vinegar is a weak acid. What does the term 'strong' refer to?
o: How completely the acid ionizes in water
How many hydrogen atoms each molecule holds
How concentrated the acid solution is
How much base is needed to neutralize it
S.w: Acid strength refers to the degree of ionization: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely in water, while a weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partially.

n.1: The number of hydrogen atoms does not set strength; acetic acid (CH₃COOH) has four hydrogens but is weak.
n.2: Concentration is how much acid is dissolved in a volume; a strong acid can be dilute and a weak acid concentrated.
n.3: The amount of base needed depends on the moles of acid present, not on whether the acid is strong or weak.

S.q: A study reporting that a sports drink improves endurance was paid for by the company that makes the drink. Eight cyclists were randomly assigned to the drink or a look-alike placebo, and the testers did not know who drank which. Which concerns are most relevant when evaluating this study?
o: Conflict of interest and no placebo group
No blinding and a conflict of interest
Conflict of interest and a small sample
No random assignment and a small sample
S.w: When evaluating a claim, ask whether the source is unbiased and the sample is large enough. Funding from the drink's maker is a conflict of interest, and 8 participants is easily skewed by chance. The design itself used random assignment, a placebo and blinding.

n.0: The other cyclists drank a look-alike placebo, so the study did have a placebo control.
n.1: The testers did not know who drank which, so the measurements were blinded; only the conflict of interest applies.
n.3: The cyclists were randomly assigned to groups, so assignment bias is not the concern; only the small sample is.

S.q: Place the links in the chain of infection in order, starting with the infectious agent and ending with the person who becomes infected.
o: Mode of transmission
Susceptible host
Infectious agent
Reservoir
Portal of exit
Portal of entry
S.w: The pathogen (infectious agent) lives in a reservoir, leaves through a portal of exit, travels by a mode of transmission, enters a new host through a portal of entry, and infects a susceptible host. Breaking any link stops the spread.

S.q: Sodium, a reactive metal, combines with chlorine, a nonmetal, to form sodium chloride (NaCl), the main salt in normal saline. Which statement correctly describes the bond in NaCl?
o: Covalent, formed as the two atoms share a pair of electrons
Metallic, formed by a sea of electrons around both atoms
Ionic, formed as sodium transfers an electron to chlorine
Ionic, formed as chlorine transfers an electron to sodium
S.w: A metal and a nonmetal with a large difference in electronegativity form an ionic bond. Sodium loses its single valence electron to chlorine, producing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that are held together by electrostatic attraction.

n.0: Sharing electron pairs describes covalent bonds, which form mainly between nonmetals.
n.1: Metallic bonding holds atoms of a metal together; NaCl is a metal combined with a nonmetal.
n.3: The bond is ionic, but the electron moves from the metal (sodium) to the nonmetal (chlorine), not the other way.

S.q: A physical therapist moves a patient's thigh through flexion, abduction, rotation and circumduction at the hip, then bends and straightens the elbow at the humeroulnar joint. Which pairing correctly classifies these two synovial joints?
o: Hip: ball-and-socket; humeroulnar: pivot
Hip: ball-and-socket; humeroulnar: hinge
Hip: condyloid; humeroulnar: hinge
Hip: condyloid; humeroulnar: pivot
S.w: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint: the rounded femoral head sits in the cup-shaped acetabulum, allowing multiaxial movement including rotation and circumduction. The humeroulnar joint is a uniaxial hinge that allows flexion and extension; forearm rotation happens at the radioulnar joints, the proximal one being a pivot.

n.0: The humeroulnar joint is a hinge that allows only flexion and extension; the pivot joint at the elbow is the proximal radioulnar joint, which rotates the radius.
n.2: The hip is not condyloid: condyloid (ellipsoid) joints such as the wrist are biaxial and do not allow true rotation, which the hip performs.
n.3: Both are misclassified: a condyloid joint cannot rotate as the hip does, and the humeroulnar joint is a hinge, not the radioulnar pivot.

S.q: A flexible, sealed balloon is moved from a warm kitchen into a freezer. The pressure on the balloon stays about the same. What happens to the balloon, and which gas law describes this change?
o: It expands, as described by Charles's law
It shrinks, as described by Boyle's law
It expands, as described by Gay-Lussac's law
It shrinks, as described by Charles's law
S.w: Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its kelvin temperature. Cooling the gas slows its particles, so the balloon shrinks.

n.0: Charles's law is the right law, but volume falls when temperature falls, so the balloon shrinks.
n.1: The balloon shrinks, but Boyle's law relates pressure and volume at constant temperature; here temperature changes at constant pressure.
n.2: Gay-Lussac's law relates pressure and temperature at constant volume, and a cooled gas does not expand.

S.q: The pancreas has an exocrine part and an endocrine part. Which of these products is released through ducts into the duodenum rather than into the blood?
o: Somatostatin made by delta cells
Insulin made by beta cells
Glucagon made by alpha cells
Trypsinogen made by acinar cells
S.w: Acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas make pancreatic juice, including trypsinogen, which travels through ducts to the duodenum. Islet hormones enter the blood.

n.0: Somatostatin is an islet hormone that acts on other islet cells; it is not part of pancreatic juice.
n.1: Insulin is an endocrine hormone from the islets and enters the blood, not a duct.
n.2: Glucagon is an islet hormone secreted into the blood to raise blood glucose.

S.q: A tissue sample taken just beneath the epidermis contains blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles and a dense mesh of collagen and elastin fibers. Which layer and tissue type does it show?
o: Smooth muscle tissue of the dermis
Connective tissue of the dermis
Epithelial tissue of the epidermis
Adipose tissue of the hypodermis
S.w: The dermis lies beneath the epidermis and is connective tissue: areolar in the papillary layer and dense irregular in the reticular layer, rich in collagen (strength) and elastin (stretch), with vessels, nerves, follicles and glands.

n.0: The dermis does contain tiny arrector pili muscles, but its main tissue is connective tissue, not smooth muscle.
n.2: The epidermis is avascular stratified squamous epithelium; it has no blood vessels or collagen mesh.
n.3: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is mostly fat with areolar tissue, not a dense collagen and elastin mesh.

S.q: Which organ, not usually listed among the classic endocrine glands, secretes erythropoietin (EPO) to stimulate red blood cell production?
o: Heart
Kidney
Spleen
Red bone marrow
S.w: The kidneys secrete erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red blood cell production.

n.0: The heart's atria secrete ANP, which lowers blood volume and pressure, not EPO.
n.2: The spleen removes old red blood cells from circulation; it does not secrete EPO.
n.3: Red bone marrow makes red blood cells in response to EPO; it does not secrete the hormone.

S.q: Reaction rate at five substrate concentrations, with enzyme amount held constant: 1 mM, 10; 2 mM, 18; 4 mM, 28; 8 mM, 33; 16 mM, 34 (rate in units per minute). What is the best prediction for the rate at 32 mM?
o: About 34, since the rate has nearly leveled off
About 44, since the rate keeps rising by a steady amount
About 68, since doubling substrate doubles the rate
About 20, since the rate falls once past an optimum
S.w: The rate rises quickly and then plateaus: from 8 to 16 mM it gains only 1 unit because the enzyme molecules are nearly saturated. Doubling the substrate again should leave the rate close to 34.

n.1: The increases shrink (8, 10, 5, 1), so the rate is leveling off, not rising steadily.
n.2: Doubling 16 mM to 32 mM does not double the rate; going from 8 to 16 mM added only 1 unit.
n.3: A rise-then-fall curve fits enzyme activity against temperature or pH, not against substrate concentration.

S.q: Counting the carpals, metacarpals and phalanges, how many bones form the skeleton of one adult hand, from the wrist to the fingertips? Enter a whole number.

tr.26: using 7 carpals, which is the number of tarsals in the foot (7 + 5 + 14)
tr.28: giving the thumb 3 phalanges like the other fingers (8 + 5 + 15)

S.w: 8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges = 27. The thumb has 2 phalanges and each of the other four fingers has 3, so the phalanges total 2 + (4 x 3) = 14.

S.q: Liver cells of a patient who takes a daily anticonvulsant drug show a marked increase in an organelle that detoxifies drugs and makes lipids. Which organelle is it?
o: Golgi apparatus
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Nucleolus
S.w: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and carries out lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification, which is why it is prominent in liver cells exposed to drugs.

n.0: The Golgi modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids; it does not detoxify drugs.
n.2: Rough ER makes proteins on its ribosomes; detoxification and lipid synthesis are smooth ER jobs.
n.3: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits inside the nucleus.

S.q: A patient receives a large volume of intravenous fluid, and the increased blood volume stretches the walls of the heart's atria. Which response helps return blood volume toward normal?
o: ADH is released, adding aquaporins to collecting ducts
Renin is released, increasing angiotensin II
ANP is released, increasing sodium and water excretion
ANP is released, increasing sodium reabsorption
S.w: Stretched atria release atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), which makes the kidneys lose more sodium and water, lowering blood volume and blood pressure: the opposite of RAAS.

n.0: ADH increases water reabsorption, which would raise blood volume further.
n.1: Renin and angiotensin II raise blood volume and pressure, which would worsen the overload.
n.3: ANP is the right hormone, but it increases sodium excretion; sodium reabsorption is aldosterone's effect.

S.q: Which statements about the transport of respiratory gases in the blood are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: About 98% of O₂ travels bound to hemoglobin
Most oxygen travels dissolved in the plasma
Most CO₂ travels bound to hemoglobin
One hemoglobin carries up to four O₂
Most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate in plasma
S.w: About 98.5% of O₂ rides on hemoglobin, and each hemoglobin carries up to 4 O₂. About 70% of CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate in plasma.

n.1: Only about 1.5% of oxygen is dissolved; most is bound to hemoglobin.
n.2: Only about 20-23% of CO₂ is bound to hemoglobin; most travels as bicarbonate.

S.q: During a 10-second sprint, a runner quickly uses up the ATP already stored in the leg muscles. Which source then regenerates ATP most rapidly for the next several seconds?
o: Oxygen stored on myoglobin
Aerobic respiration in mitochondria
Creatine phosphate
Anaerobic glycolysis
S.w: Muscle energy sources come into play in sequence: stored ATP (a few seconds), then creatine phosphate, which transfers its phosphate to ADP almost instantly (about 10 to 15 seconds), then anaerobic glycolysis, then aerobic respiration.

n.0: Myoglobin stores oxygen for aerobic respiration; it does not regenerate ATP directly.
n.1: Aerobic respiration yields the most ATP but is the slowest pathway, so it is not the most rapid source.
n.3: Anaerobic glycolysis is fast but follows creatine phosphate as the main source after the first several seconds.

S.q: A patient who spends almost no time outdoors develops low blood calcium. Which sequence best describes the skin's normal role in calcium absorption from the intestine?
o: Melanocytes secrete vitamin D3 after UVB exposure; the kidneys then activate it
UVB converts a cholesterol derivative directly into active calcitriol in skin
Sebaceous glands secrete vitamin D3 in sebum; the liver then activates it
UVB makes vitamin D3 from a cholesterol derivative; liver and kidneys activate it
S.w: Step 1: in the skin, UVB converts a cholesterol derivative to vitamin D3, an inactive precursor. Step 2: the liver and kidneys convert it to active calcitriol, which increases calcium absorption from the gut. Little sun means little D3 and poorer Ca²⁺ absorption.

n.0: Melanocytes make melanin, which absorbs UV; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative in the skin, and the liver also takes part in activation.
n.1: The skin makes only the precursor; activation to calcitriol takes place in the liver and kidneys.
n.2: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum to lubricate skin; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative, and the kidneys also take part in activation.

S.q: A student's carefully controlled experiment produces data that do not support her hypothesis. According to the scientific method, what is the most appropriate response?
o: Report the results and revise the hypothesis for further testing
Reword the hypothesis to fit the data and report it as confirmed
Discard the results because the experiment did not work
Repeat the same trial until one result supports the hypothesis
S.w: Results that fail to support a hypothesis are still valid findings. The scientist reports them, revises the hypothesis and tests again; science is iterative.

n.1: A hypothesis rewritten after seeing the data has not been tested by those data, so it cannot be called confirmed.
n.2: A controlled experiment that rejects a hypothesis has worked; negative results are informative.
n.3: Repeating until a favorable result appears is cherry-picking, which biases the conclusion.

S.q: Researchers hypothesize that caffeine shortens reaction time in well-rested adults. Volunteers were assigned to five groups before a reaction-time test. Select the conditions of the group that serves as the control for testing this hypothesis.

sn.g1: Group 1 Before the test 100 mg caffeine, 8 h sleep
sn.g2: Group 2 Before the test 0 mg caffeine, 4 h sleep
sn.g3: Group 3 Before the test 0 mg caffeine, 8 h sleep
sn.g4: Group 4 Before the test 200 mg caffeine, 8 h sleep
sn.g5: Group 5 Before the test 200 mg caffeine, 4 h sleep

S.w: A control group matches the experimental groups in every way except the independent variable, and it receives none of the treatment. The hypothesis is about well-rested adults, so the control gets no caffeine and a full 8 hours of sleep (Group 3). Comparing it with Groups 1 and 4 isolates the effect of caffeine.

n.g1: Group 1 received caffeine, so it is an experimental group.
n.g2: Group 2 received no caffeine, but it was not well rested. Sleep loss itself changes reaction time, so this group cannot serve as the baseline for well-rested adults.
n.g4: Group 4 received the highest dose of caffeine, so it is an experimental group.
n.g5: Group 5 changed two factors at once (caffeine and sleep), so it cannot serve as the baseline for either.

S.q: During meiosis I in a woman's ovary, the two copies of chromosome 21 fail to separate, and both end up in the egg. A normal sperm fertilizes this egg. What will the zygote most likely have?
o: 47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21
47 chromosomes, with an XXY set of sex chromosomes
45 chromosomes, with one copy of chromosome 21
45 chromosomes, the pattern seen in Turner syndrome
S.w: Step 1: nondisjunction gives the egg 24 chromosomes, including two copies of chromosome 21. Step 2: adding a normal sperm's 23 gives 47, with three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21, Down syndrome).

n.1: XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) involves the sex chromosomes, but the nondisjunction here involved chromosome 21.
n.2: A zygote with one chromosome 21 would come from an egg that received no copy. Here the egg received both copies.
n.3: Turner syndrome (45,X) is a missing sex chromosome. This egg has an extra chromosome, so the total rises above 46.

S.q: A 56-year-old woman has gone through menopause, and her ovaries no longer contain functioning follicles. Which pattern of hormone levels is expected in her blood?
o: High estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with high FSH and LH
Low estrogen with high progesterone and low FSH
S.w: Two steps. (1) With the follicles exhausted, the ovaries make little estrogen and progesterone. (2) Those hormones normally exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so without them FSH and LH rise.

n.0: Without functioning follicles the ovaries cannot keep estrogen and progesterone high.
n.1: Falling ovarian hormones remove negative feedback, so FSH and LH rise rather than fall.
n.3: Progesterone comes mainly from the corpus luteum, which forms after ovulation, so it is low after menopause; FSH is high.

S.q: Around day 26 of a 28-day cycle with no pregnancy, progesterone falls sharply. Select the structure whose lining breaks down and is shed as a result.
S.w: Progesterone from the corpus luteum keeps the secretory endometrium thick and glandular. Without hCG from an embryo, the corpus luteum degenerates about 10 to 12 days after ovulation; progesterone falls, the spiral arteries constrict, and the functional layer of the endometrium breaks down and is shed as menstrual flow.

n.ovary: The corpus luteum in the ovary degenerates and causes the fall in progesterone. That is the cause, not the result, and ovarian tissue is not shed as menstrual flow.
n.tube: The uterine tube carries the oocyte or embryo toward the uterus. Its lining is not shed in menstruation.
n.cervix: The cervix is the lower neck of the uterus that menstrual flow passes through. Its lining is not the tissue that is shed.
n.vagina: The vagina is the outlet for menstrual flow. Its lining is not shed when progesterone falls.

S.q: Fresh milk scatters a beam of light shone through it, and its tiny dispersed particles do not settle out even after the milk stands for hours. How is milk best classified?
o: A solution
A suspension
A compound
A colloid
S.w: A colloid is a mixture whose dispersed particles are larger than in a solution but do not settle; they scatter light (the Tyndall effect). Milk, fog and gelatin are colloids.

n.0: Solution particles are too small to scatter a light beam; a true solution looks clear.
n.1: Suspension particles are large enough to settle out on standing and can be filtered.
n.2: Milk is a mixture of many substances in variable proportions, not a single compound with a fixed ratio.

S.q: A diagram shows a patient facing the viewer, and an instructor points to the lower abdominal quadrant on the viewer's left side. Which organ is located in that quadrant?
o: The spleen
The appendix
The gallbladder
The sigmoid colon
S.w: Two steps: a patient facing the viewer has their right side on the viewer's left, so the instructor is pointing to the patient's right lower quadrant (RLQ), which contains the appendix and cecum.

n.0: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant, not a lower quadrant.
n.2: The gallbladder is in the right upper quadrant, under the liver, not a lower quadrant.
n.3: The sigmoid colon is in the left lower quadrant. That is the patient's left, which appears on the viewer's right.

S.q: Magnesium, an element needed for muscle and nerve function, has atomic number 12. Which arrangement of electrons, listed by shell from the nucleus outward, describes a neutral magnesium atom?
S.w: Electrons fill the lowest shells first. The first shell holds 2 and the second holds 8, which accounts for 10 electrons; the remaining 2 go into the third shell: 2, 8, 2. Magnesium therefore has 2 valence electrons, matching its place in group 2.

n.0: The second shell fills to 8 before any electrons enter the third shell.
n.1: The third shell can hold more than 1 electron, so both remaining electrons go into it rather than starting a fourth shell.
n.3: The second shell holds a maximum of 8 electrons, so it cannot hold 10.

S.q: A cell has a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall, but no chloroplasts. Of the following, which is the most likely source of this cell?
o: A yeast cell
A Staphylococcus bacterium
A moss leaf cell
A human liver cell
S.w: Step 1: a nucleus and mitochondria mean the cell is eukaryotic, which rules out bacteria. Step 2: a cell wall without chloroplasts fits a fungus such as yeast, which has a chitin wall and cannot photosynthesize.

n.1: Bacteria have cell walls but are prokaryotes, so they have no nucleus or mitochondria.
n.2: A moss leaf cell has a wall and nucleus, but as a photosynthetic leaf cell it contains chloroplasts.
n.3: Human cells are eukaryotic with mitochondria, but animal cells have no cell wall.

S.q: A histology lab compares the three muscle types. Which description matches smooth muscle, such as the muscle found in the wall of the small intestine?
o: Spindle-shaped cells, one nucleus, nonstriated, involuntary
Branched cells, intercalated discs, striated, involuntary
Long cylindrical cells, many nuclei, striated, voluntary
Spindle-shaped cells, many nuclei, striated, voluntary
S.w: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped (fusiform) with one nucleus, lack striations and are under involuntary control by the autonomic nervous system and hormones. They produce slow, sustained contractions such as peristalsis.

n.1: Branched, striated, involuntary cells joined by intercalated discs describe cardiac muscle.
n.2: Long, cylindrical, multinucleated, striated, voluntary fibers describe skeletal muscle.
n.3: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, but they have one nucleus, no striations and involuntary control.

S.q: Blood is allowed to clot in a tube, and the clear fluid above the clot (serum) is collected. Which component of plasma is missing from the serum?
o: Glucose
Fibrinogen
Antibodies
Albumin
S.w: Serum is plasma without the clotting factors. Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin and used up in the clot, so it is absent from serum.

n.0: Glucose is a dissolved nutrient that stays in the serum.
n.2: Antibodies (globulins) are not used in clotting and remain in the serum.
n.3: Albumin does not take part in clotting, so it remains in the serum.

S.q: A cook notices that olive oil forms a separate layer on water but dissolves easily in hexane, a liquid made of nonpolar molecules. Which statement explains this behavior?
o: Hexane is denser than water, so it holds more dissolved oil
Nonpolar oil dissolves in nonpolar hexane but not in polar water
Oil is an ionic compound that dissolves best in hexane
Polar oil dissolves in polar hexane but not in nonpolar water
S.w: 'Like dissolves like': nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents, and polar or ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents. Oil is nonpolar, so it mixes with hexane but not with polar water.

n.0: Density decides which layer floats, not whether a substance dissolves; hexane is actually less dense than water.
n.2: Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents such as water, not in nonpolar hexane; oil is nonpolar and molecular.
n.3: The rule is applied correctly, but the labels are reversed: oil and hexane are nonpolar, and water is polar.

S.q: An electronic balance shows 0.20 g with nothing on the pan, but a student does not zero it. Each of five samples is then recorded 0.20 g heavier than its true mass. Which best describes this error?
o: Systematic error, which reduces accuracy
Systematic error, which reduces precision
Random error, which reduces precision
Random error, which reduces accuracy
S.w: An error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction is systematic. It moves the results away from the true values, so it reduces accuracy; the readings can still agree with each other.

n.1: A constant offset does not spread the readings out, so precision is unaffected; accuracy is what suffers.
n.2: Random error varies unpredictably from reading to reading; a constant 0.20 g offset is not random.
n.3: The error is identical every time, so it is systematic, not random.

S.q: On an energy diagram for a reaction, the curve rises from the reactants to a peak and then falls to the products. What does the height from the reactants up to the peak represent?
o: The activation energy needed to start the reaction
The change in energy between reactants and products
The total energy released by the reaction
The energy stored in the bonds of the products
S.w: The 'hill' between the reactants and the peak is the activation energy, the minimum energy colliding particles need to react. A catalyst lowers this peak.

n.1: The overall energy change (delta H) is the difference between the reactant and product levels, which does not include the peak.
n.2: The energy released is the drop from the reactants down to the products, not the rise to the peak.
n.3: The energy of the products is the level of the curve after the peak, not the height of the climb.

S.q: A student is identifying substances whose molecules contain polar covalent bonds, where electrons are shared unequally. Which substances contain polar covalent bonds? Select all that apply.
o: Hydrogen gas (H₂)
Ammonia (NH₃)
Chlorine gas (Cl₂)
Oxygen gas (O₂) from a medical cylinder
Hydrogen chloride (HCl)
Water (H₂O)
S.w: Bonds between two different nonmetals with different electronegativities are polar covalent: O-H in water, N-H in ammonia and H-Cl in hydrogen chloride.

n.0: Both atoms in H₂ are identical, so they share electrons equally: a nonpolar covalent bond.
n.2: Cl₂ is made of two identical atoms, so its bond is nonpolar covalent.
n.3: O₂ has two identical atoms sharing electrons equally, so its bond is nonpolar.

S.q: A student examines a wilting houseplant on a windowsill and writes four statements in her lab notebook. Which statement is an observation rather than an inference?
o: The plant is not getting enough nitrogen.
The roots have probably started to rot.
The plant was overwatered sometime last week.
The lower leaves are yellow with brown edges.
S.w: An observation is what is directly seen or measured: leaf color can be seen. The other statements interpret the observations to explain a cause, which makes them inferences.

n.0: A nitrogen shortage is an explanation inferred from the yellow leaves; it was not directly observed.
n.1: Root rot is a guess about a hidden part of the plant, so it is an inference.
n.2: Past overwatering is a possible cause the student is inferring, not something she saw.

S.q: Place the levels of protein structure in order, starting with the simplest level and ending with the most complex.
o: R-group interactions fold the chain into its overall 3-D shape.
Hydrogen bonds along the backbone form helices and pleated sheets.
Amino acids are linked in a specific sequence by peptide bonds.
Two or more folded polypeptide chains join, as in hemoglobin.
S.w: Primary (amino acid sequence) -> secondary (alpha helix and beta pleated sheet from backbone hydrogen bonds) -> tertiary (overall 3-D shape from R-group interactions) -> quaternary (two or more chains, such as the four chains of hemoglobin).

S.q: The systemic circulation begins in which chamber of the heart, and to which chamber does it return blood?
o: It begins in the right ventricle and returns blood to the left atrium
It begins in the left ventricle and returns blood to the right atrium
It begins in the left atrium and returns blood to the right ventricle
It begins in the left ventricle and returns blood to the left atrium
S.w: Systemic circulation: left ventricle to aorta, body tissues and venae cavae, ending in the right atrium. Pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium.

n.0: Right ventricle to left atrium describes the pulmonary circulation.
n.2: Atria receive blood rather than pump it into a circuit; the systemic circuit starts at the left ventricle.
n.3: Systemic blood returns through the venae cavae to the right atrium, not the left.

S.q: A student describes an unknown element as dull, brittle in its solid form, and a poor conductor of heat and electricity. In which region of the periodic table is this element most likely found?
o: The left side, among the alkali metals
The center, among the transition metals
The staircase line, among the metalloids
The upper right, among the nonmetals
S.w: Dull luster, brittleness and poor conductivity are the properties of nonmetals, which are found in the upper right of the periodic table (plus hydrogen).

n.0: Alkali metals are shiny, soft metals that conduct heat and electricity well.
n.1: Transition metals are shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors.
n.2: Metalloids have intermediate properties and are semiconductors; they conduct better than typical nonmetals.

S.q: During a panic attack, a student breathes rapidly and deeply for several minutes. Using CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, what happens in her blood?
o: CO₂ builds up, the reaction shifts right, H⁺ rises and pH falls
CO₂ is blown off, the reaction shifts left, H⁺ falls and pH rises
CO₂ is blown off, the reaction shifts right, H⁺ rises and pH falls
CO₂ is blown off, the reaction shifts left, H⁺ falls and pH falls
S.w: Step 1: hyperventilation removes CO₂ faster than it is made. Step 2: with less CO₂, the equilibrium shifts left, using up H⁺; fewer H⁺ ions means a higher pH (respiratory alkalosis).

n.0: CO₂ builds up with slow, shallow breathing, not with rapid deep breathing.
n.2: Removing a reactant (CO₂) shifts the equilibrium left, not right, so H⁺ falls.
n.3: The shift and the fall in H⁺ are right, but fewer H⁺ ions means pH rises.

S.q: Research journals require scientists to describe their methods in enough detail for other researchers to follow. What is the main scientific purpose of this requirement?
o: It lets readers apply the results to any population.
It lets editors judge the authors' expertise and reputation.
It lets reviewers confirm that the hypothesis has been proven.
It lets other scientists repeat the work and check the results.
S.w: Scientific explanations must be reproducible. Detailed methods let independent scientists replicate the study, and peer review and replication check whether the conclusions hold.

n.0: Detailed methods show exactly who and what was studied, which limits the conclusions to that population rather than extending them.
n.1: Judging a claim by the authors' authority is not evidence; methods are described so the work itself can be checked.
n.2: Evidence supports a hypothesis but never proves it; methods are shared so the work can be checked, and possibly refuted.

S.q: Stretch receptors in the bladder wall signal that the bladder is full. The signal travels to the spinal cord, and the reply makes the smooth muscle of the bladder wall contract. Which fibers carried the incoming and outgoing signals?
o: Afferent fibers in; somatic motor fibers out
Afferent fibers in; sympathetic fibers out
Afferent fibers in; parasympathetic fibers out
Efferent fibers in; parasympathetic fibers out
S.w: Two steps: incoming sensory signals travel on afferent fibers, and contraction of the bladder's smooth muscle to promote urination is a parasympathetic (autonomic motor) effect.

n.0: Somatic motor fibers control skeletal muscle; the bladder wall is smooth muscle under autonomic control.
n.1: The sympathetic division slows urination; the parasympathetic division contracts the bladder wall.
n.3: Signals entering the CNS travel on afferent fibers; efferent fibers carry commands out.

S.q: A genetics counselor reviews the ABO blood types of four couples. Which couple cannot have a child with type O blood?
o: Type AB (IAIB) and type O (ii)
Type A (IAi) and type O (ii)
Type A (IAi) and type B (IBi)
Type O (ii) and type O (ii)
S.w: A type O child must be ii, receiving i from each parent. A type AB parent (IAIB) has no i allele, so this couple can have only A (IAi) or B (IBi) children.

n.1: Both parents carry i, so an ii child (1/2 chance) is possible.
n.2: Both parents carry i, so an ii child (1/4 chance) is possible.
n.3: ii x ii gives ii children, all type O.

S.q: Place the events of DNA replication in the order they occur at a replication fork, starting with the first.
o: DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments together.
Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds.
Primase lays down a short RNA primer.
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides.
S.w: Helicase unzips the double helix; primase adds an RNA primer; DNA polymerase extends from the primer, adding complementary nucleotides 5' to 3' and proofreading; on the lagging strand the resulting Okazaki fragments are joined by DNA ligase.

S.q: Before a newly made pre-mRNA leaves the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, it is processed. Which change occurs during this processing?
o: Introns are removed and exons are joined.
Codons are translated into amino acids.
Thymine bases are replaced by uracil.
Exons are removed and introns are joined.
S.w: During processing, introns (noncoding regions) are cut out and exons (coding regions) are spliced together; a 5' cap and poly-A tail are also added.

n.1: Translation happens later, at ribosomes in the cytoplasm, after the mRNA leaves the nucleus.
n.2: RNA is built with uracil from the start; no thymine is present in pre-mRNA to replace.
n.3: This is reversed: introns are removed and exons are kept.

S.q: Select the region that contains the vital centers that set the basic rhythm of breathing and regulate heart rate and blood pressure.
S.w: The medulla oblongata, the lowest part of the brainstem and continuous with the spinal cord, holds the cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centers. It sets the basic breathing rhythm and adjusts heart rate and blood pressure, which is why injury here is so dangerous.

n.pons: The pons, just above the medulla, helps smooth the breathing pattern and relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum, but the rhythm-setting and cardiovascular centers are in the medulla.
n.cerebellum: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture. It holds no vital centers.
n.frontal: The frontal lobe controls voluntary movement, planning and judgment, not automatic vital functions.

E.q: A student is checking notes from a clinical rotation. Which of the following is a fragment?
o: Hoping to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
She hoped to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
Finish your charting before the end of the shift.
Hoping to finish, she charted before the end of the shift.
E.w: Two steps: "Hoping" is a participle, not a main verb, and the word group has no subject, so it cannot stand alone.

n.1: This has a subject (She) and a main verb (hoped), so it is complete.
n.2: This is an imperative sentence; its subject "you" is understood, so it is complete.
n.3: The participial phrase is attached to the independent clause "she charted ...", so it is complete.

E.q: Luis is writing an argumentative essay about school start times. Which sentence would work best as his thesis statement?
o: In this essay, I will discuss the start times of high schools across the country.
Many high schools in the United States begin classes before 8:30 in the morning.
High schools should start after 8:30 a.m. to improve teens' sleep and grades.
Should high schools start later in the morning so that teenagers get more sleep?
E.w: An effective thesis makes one specific, arguable claim and can preview the main points. This sentence takes a clear position (start after 8:30 a.m.) and names the reasons the essay will develop (sleep and grades).

n.0: This is an announcement of the topic ("In this essay, I will"); it states no position for the essay to argue.
n.1: This is a statement of fact that no one would dispute, so there is nothing to argue.
n.3: A question is not a thesis; the thesis should answer the question with a claim.

E.q: Read the passage about a hospital stay. Select the word or phrase that contains a capitalization error.

parts.t: uncle
Mercy General Hospital
Doctor
Mom
Nurse Patel

parts: brought us a printed copy of his care plan and showed us where to find the family lounge.

E.w: A title is capitalized when it comes directly before a name or replaces a name in direct address. "The doctor" is a general reference to a person's job, so it should be lowercase.

n.a: After a possessive (my uncle), a family word is a common noun and stays lowercase.
n.b: The full name of a specific hospital is a proper noun, so every main word is capitalized.
n.d: Mom is used as a name here (it could be replaced by her first name), so it is capitalized.
n.e: Nurse is a title placed directly before a name, so it is capitalized.

E.q: After a long flight, a patient developed pain and redness in her calf, and an ultrasound confirmed thrombophlebitis. Using all of its word parts, what does thrombophlebitis mean?
o: Vein hardening caused by a blood clot
Surgical removal of a clot in a vein
Vein inflammation with a blood clot
Artery inflammation with a blood clot
E.w: Step 1: thromb/o means clot and phleb/o means vein. Step 2: -itis means inflammation. Together: inflammation of a vein associated with a blood clot.

n.0: Hardening is -sclerosis; -itis means inflammation.
n.1: Removal is -ectomy (thrombectomy); -itis means inflammation.
n.3: Artery is arteri/o; phleb/o means vein.

E.q: The physician told the unit clerk that she would dictate her notes on each patient after morning rounds. Based on its root, what will the physician do with her notes?
o: Look them over for errors
Say them aloud for recording
Send them on to another office
Write them out by hand
E.w: The root dict means say, so to dictate is to say words aloud for someone (or a device) to record.

n.0: Looking is the meaning of spec/spect (as in inspect).
n.2: Sending is the meaning of mit/mis (as in transmit).
n.3: Writing is the meaning of scrib/script (as in prescription).

E.q: A nurse is confirming paperwork with a patient. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Ms. Chen, you finished, the intake form didn't you?
Ms. Chen you finished the intake form, didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form, didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form didn't you?
E.w: A name in direct address is set off by a comma, and a tag question (didn't you?) is also set off by a comma.

n.0: A comma must not separate the verb (finished) from its object, and the comma before the tag question is missing.
n.1: The comma after the name in direct address is missing.
n.3: The comma before the tag question "didn't you" is missing.

E.q: Read the sentence from a pharmacy incident report: "If the order had been clearer, the pharmacy could of filled it on time." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "could of filled" to "could have filled" and "had been" to "would have been."
Change "could of filled" to "could have filled."
Change "had been" to "was."
Change "could of filled" to "could had filled."
E.w: "Could of" is a mishearing of "could've." The correct form is "could have" + past participle: "could have filled."

n.0: This fixes "could of" but adds a new error: the if-clause of a past unreal condition takes "had been," not "would have been."
n.2: "Had been" is correct for a past condition that did not happen, and the "could of" error would remain.
n.3: "Could" is a helping verb and must be followed by the base form "have"; "could had filled" is ungrammatical.

E.q: A student is writing a persuasive paragraph for a nursing program application and must use formal written English. Which sentence uses the subjunctive mood correctly?
o: If I was the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I were the instructor, I will allow one retake per exam.
If I would be the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I were the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
E.w: For an unreal or hypothetical condition, formal English uses "were" for all subjects and "would" in the main clause.

n.0: A condition contrary to fact takes the subjunctive "were" in formal writing, not "was."
n.1: An unreal "if I were" condition pairs with "would," not the future "will."
n.2: "Would" belongs in the result clause, not the if-clause; use "If I were."

E.q: As Owen drafts an essay on hospital volunteering, a classmate tells him to stop and look up the spelling of each unfamiliar word as soon as he types it. Based on the writing process, what is the best advice for Owen?
o: Keep drafting, and check the spelling later during editing
Keep drafting, and check the spelling later during revising
Keep drafting, and leave the spelling for the publishing stage
Stop drafting, since spelling must be fixed before revising
E.w: Drafting focuses on getting ideas down in sentences and paragraphs, not on perfection. Spelling is a sentence-level correction handled during editing (and the final proofread), which comes after revising and before publishing.

n.1: Revising deals with content and organization (adding, moving and cutting material); spelling is a sentence-level fix that belongs to editing.
n.2: Publishing is submitting or sharing the final copy; spelling must already be corrected by then, during editing and the final proofread.
n.3: Spelling is checked during editing, which comes after revising, not before it; stopping to fix each word while drafting interrupts the flow of ideas.

E.q: A patient with repeated attacks of pain from gallstones is scheduled for a cholecystectomy next week. Using all of its word parts, what will the surgeon do?
o: Examine the gallbladder
Remove the gallbladder
Remove the urinary bladder
Cut into the gallbladder
E.w: Step 1: chol/e means bile and cyst/o means bladder or sac, so cholecyst is the bile sac (gallbladder). Step 2: -ectomy means surgical removal. A cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder.

n.0: Visual examination is -scopy, not -ectomy.
n.2: cyst/o alone can mean the urinary bladder, but chol/e (bile) makes this the gallbladder.
n.3: Cutting into an organ is -otomy, not -ectomy.

E.q: Read the clinic notice. Select the word that is spelled incorrectly.

parts: Starting next month, the clinic will

parts.t: accommodate
Wednesday
received
schedule
occured
noticeable

parts: rise in demand. Patients who arrive after 11 a.m. may be asked to return in the afternoon.

E.w: Occur ends in a stressed syllable (oc-CUR) with a single vowel before a single final consonant, so the r doubles before a vowel suffix: occurred.

n.a: Accommodate has a double c and a double m. It is spelled correctly.
n.b: Wednesday keeps its silent d. It is spelled correctly.
n.c: The rule "i before e except after c" gives receive and received. It is spelled correctly.
n.f: Noticeable keeps the silent e after the soft c before -able, so the c keeps its s sound. It is spelled correctly.

E.q: A nurse is documenting what a worried parent asked at the bedside. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?".
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked "is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished"?
E.w: The quoted words are a question, so the question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark, and it also ends the sentence; no second end mark is added.

n.0: The question mark already ends the sentence; adding a period doubles the end punctuation.
n.2: A comma should introduce the quotation, and the quoted sentence should begin with a capital letter.
n.3: The question mark belongs to the quotation, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark.

E.q: Read the paragraph from a county health report. (1) In 2015, the county had one free clinic. (2) By 2020, it had three, plus a mobile health van. (3) Last year, two more clinics opened in rural towns. (4) Access to free health care in the county has grown steadily over the past decade. Which sentence is the topic sentence?
o: Sentence 2
Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 3
E.w: This paragraph moves from specific to general: the details come first, and sentence 4 states the main idea they support.

n.0: Sentence 2 is another specific detail about the number of clinics in 2020.
n.1: Sentence 1 is a specific detail (one clinic in 2015); being first does not make it the main idea.
n.3: Sentence 3 is a specific detail about last year's openings.

E.q: A student is writing up a chemistry lab for a formal report. Which sentence uses the most precise wording?
o: The sample was heated for 10 minutes until it reached 80 degrees Celsius.
The sample was heated briefly until it reached a high temperature.
The sample was heated for several minutes until it reached 80 degrees Celsius.
The sample was heated for 10 minutes until it became very hot.
E.w: Precise word choice gives exact, specific information. A lab report should state measured values, not vague impressions.

n.1: "Briefly" and "a high temperature" sound formal but give no measurable information.
n.2: The temperature is exact, but "several minutes" is vague; a lab report needs the measured time.
n.3: The time is exact, but "very hot" is vague; a lab report needs the measured temperature.

E.q: A patient leaflet about a vaccine reads: "___ the vaccine can cause a sore arm, most patients find this side effect mild and brief." Which word or phrase best completes the sentence?
o: Because
Whenever
Unless
Although
E.w: The sentence concedes a drawback (a sore arm) and then plays it down. "Although" signals concession.

n.0: "Because" signals cause, but a sore arm does not cause the side effect to be mild.
n.1: "Whenever" signals time, which does not fit a possible side effect weighed against its mildness.
n.2: "Unless" signals a condition, which makes the sentence illogical.

E.q: A unit has twelve patients, and only one of them fell yesterday. Which sentence correctly identifies that particular patient?
o: The patient who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
E.w: Two steps: with twelve patients, "who fell yesterday" is essential (restrictive) because it identifies which patient. Essential clauses take no commas.

n.1: A comma must not separate the subject from its verb (needs).
n.2: A single comma after "patient" opens an aside that is never closed.
n.3: Commas would mark the clause as nonessential, as if there were only one patient; here it is needed to identify the patient.

E.q: A nurse manager is writing a formal report to a hospital's board of directors: "The pilot program cut readmissions by 12 percent, which is a pretty big deal for a unit of our size." Which phrase should be revised?
o: the pilot program
a pretty big deal
cut readmissions
by 12 percent
E.w: "A pretty big deal" is slang. A formal report needs precise wording such as "a significant improvement for a unit of our size."

n.0: "The pilot program" is a precise, standard name for a trial program.
n.2: "Cut readmissions" is clear and accurate; "cut" is a standard verb for a reduction.
n.3: "By 12 percent" is a specific, formal way to report the result.

E.q: Rachel's thesis states that community gardens improve neighborhood health by increasing access to fresh produce, encouraging exercise, and building social ties. Which topic sentence best fits her second body paragraph?
o: Friendships formed in community gardens can last for years.
Many cities have started community gardens in empty lots.
Community gardens make fresh produce easier for families to get.
Community gardens also give residents a reason to stay active.
E.w: Body paragraphs usually follow the order of the points previewed in the thesis. The second point is exercise, so the second body paragraph's topic sentence should introduce physical activity.

n.0: Social ties are the thesis's third point, so this belongs to the third body paragraph.
n.1: This is general background that does not develop any of the thesis's three points.
n.2: Access to produce is the thesis's first point, so it belongs to the first body paragraph.

E.q: Kayla's first draft of a research paper on nutrition labels is complete. Place the remaining tasks in the order she should complete them, starting with the first.
o: Reorganize paragraphs and strengthen weak support
Do a final read for typos and missing words
Correct subject-verb agreement and punctuation errors
Submit the final copy to the instructor
E.w: After drafting, the writer revises (reorganizes and strengthens content), then edits (grammar and punctuation), then proofreads (a final check for typos and missing words), and finally publishes (submits the paper). Big-picture changes come first so that later polishing is not wasted on text that gets cut.

E.q: Read the paragraph from a student's research summary. (1) A recent study examined how evening screen time affects sleep in adolescents. (2) Teens who used their phones after 9 p.m. got a lot less sleep. (3) On average, they slept 48 minutes less than peers who did not use phones at night. (4) These findings suggest that limiting evening screen use may improve rest. Which sentence does not match the formal register of the paragraph?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
E.w: Sentence 2 uses informal wording ("teens," "got," "a lot less"). A formal version: "Adolescents who used their phones after 9 p.m. slept less."

n.0: Sentence 1 is formal: precise terms ("adolescents," "evening screen time") and an objective tone.
n.1: Sentence 3 is formal: it reports a specific figure in standard language.
n.2: Sentence 4 is formal: "suggest" and "may" state the conclusion with appropriate caution.

E.q: A student is checking whether sentences about a retired nurse contain a dependent clause. Which sentence is complex?
o: The nurse trained me, and she retired last spring.
The nurse who trained me retired last spring.
The nurse trained me and retired last spring.
Trained by experts, the nurse retired last spring.
E.w: Two steps: "who trained me" has its own subject (who) and verb (trained), so it is a dependent relative clause; with the independent clause "The nurse retired last spring", the sentence is complex.

n.0: Two independent clauses with no dependent clause make a compound sentence.
n.2: One subject with two verbs is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.
n.3: "Trained by experts" is a participial phrase (no subject-verb pair), so the sentence is simple.

E.q: A unit manager is writing a staffing note at the end of a long shift. Which sentence uses "to," "too," and "two" correctly?
o: The two aides were too tired to finish the charts.
The too aides were too tired to finish the charts.
The two aides were too tired too finish the charts.
The two aides were to tired to finish the charts.
E.w: "Two" is the number, "too" means excessively (too tired), and "to" begins the infinitive (to finish).

n.1: The number of aides requires "two".
n.2: An infinitive is formed with "to": "to finish".
n.3: "___ tired" means excessively tired, which requires "too".

E.q: A surgical unit's family liaison is writing an update. Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly to show which action happened first?
o: The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrives.
The surgeon finishes the procedure by the time the family had arrived.
The surgeon has finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
E.w: The past perfect (had + past participle) marks the earlier of two past actions. The procedure ended first, then the family arrived.

n.1: "Arrives" is present tense, which clashes with "had finished"; both events are in the past.
n.2: The tenses are reversed: the earlier action (finishing) needs the past perfect, and the later one the simple past.
n.3: The present perfect "has finished" does not fit a completed past time frame set by "arrived"; use "had finished."

E.q: Ana's peer reviewer leaves two comments: (1) "Your second paragraph doesn't connect to your thesis," and (2) "You wrote 'effect' where you mean 'affect.'" Which statement correctly classifies the work these comments call for?
o: Both comments call for revising, since both change the draft.
Comment 1 calls for revising, and comment 2 calls for editing.
Comment 1 calls for editing, and comment 2 calls for revising.
Both comments call for proofreading, since both point out errors.
E.w: Step 1: a paragraph that does not support the thesis is a content and organization problem, so fixing it is revising. Step 2: choosing affect instead of effect is a word-usage correction at the sentence level, so fixing it is editing.

n.0: Any fix changes the draft, but a usage error like affect/effect is corrected in editing, not revising.
n.2: This swaps the two stages: connecting a paragraph to the thesis is revising, and fixing a word error is editing.
n.3: Proofreading is the last check for typos; reworking a paragraph so it supports the thesis is revising.

E.q: Read the paragraph. (1) Kayla works nights at a nursing home. (2) She checks on residents and updates their charts. (3) When a resident cannot sleep, she brings warm milk. (4) Her job is tiring, but she loves it. Which sentence is complex?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
E.w: Sentence 3 has a dependent clause (When a resident cannot sleep) and an independent clause (she brings warm milk), so it is complex.

n.0: Sentence 1 is simple: one independent clause.
n.1: Sentence 2 is simple: one subject with a compound verb (checks and updates).
n.3: Sentence 4 is compound: two independent clauses joined by ", but".

E.q: Read the sentence from a staff policy: "Staff should utilize the aforementioned procedure in order to facilitate patient egress." Which revision replaces the inflated wording with plain language and keeps the meaning?
o: Staff should use the procedure described above as needed.
Staff should use this procedure to help patients leave.
Staff should employ the stated procedure to facilitate patient egress.
Staff should use the aforementioned procedure to help patients leave.
E.w: Plain language replaces inflated words: utilize = use, facilitate = help, egress = leaving, in order to = to.

n.0: This version drops the purpose (helping patients leave), so it loses meaning.
n.2: "Employ," "facilitate" and "egress" are still inflated words for "use," "help" and "leave."
n.3: "Aforementioned" is still an inflated word; plain language would say "this procedure."

E.q: A clinic receptionist is writing questions for a new front-desk guide. Which sentence uses who or whom correctly?
o: The student whom earned the top score will speak at graduation.
Whom do you think will be named the new charge nurse?
To whom should I send the completed insurance forms?
Whom is responsible for the night count of controlled drugs?
E.w: "Whom" is the objective form. In "To whom should I send," the pronoun is the object of the preposition "to" (send them to him), so "whom" is correct.

n.0: The pronoun is the subject of "earned" (she earned), so it must be "who."
n.1: Ignore "do you think": the pronoun is the subject of "will be named" (he will be named), so it must be "Who."
n.3: The pronoun is the subject of "is responsible" (he is responsible), so it must be "Who."

E.q: A clinical instructor is reviewing four sentences from a student handbook draft. Which sentence is written with parallel structure?
o: The applicant was praised for her punctuality, her empathy, and for being skilled.
The checklist asks staff to wash hands, wear gloves, and dispose of sharps safely.
Volunteers may greet visitors, deliver flowers, or they can read to patients.
The course teaches students how to splint a fracture and controlling bleeding.
E.w: All three items after "to" are base verbs (wash, wear, dispose), so the series is parallel.

n.0: Two nouns ("her punctuality," "her empathy") are followed by a gerund phrase with a repeated "for"; it should be "and her clinical skill."
n.2: The first two items are verb phrases, but the third is a full clause ("they can read"); it should be "or read to patients."
n.3: "How to splint" is paired with the gerund "controlling"; it should be "how to splint a fracture and control bleeding."

E.q: Read the paragraph. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the paragraph's unity.

parts.t: Regular hand washing is one of the simplest ways to prevent the spread of infection in hospitals.
Germs on the hands of health care workers can travel from one patient to the next during routine care.
Washing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds removes many of these germs.
When hands are not visibly dirty, an alcohol-based sanitizer offers a quick alternative.
Some hospitals have replaced paper towels with electric hand dryers to reduce waste.
Posting reminder signs near sinks can increase how often staff clean their hands.

sn.a: Regular hand washing is one of the simplest ways to prevent the spread of infection in hospitals.
sn.b: Germs on the hands of health care workers can travel from one patient to the next during routine care.
sn.c: Washing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds removes many of these germs.
sn.e: When hands are not visibly dirty, an alcohol-based sanitizer offers a quick alternative.
sn.d: Some hospitals have replaced paper towels with electric hand dryers to reduce waste.
sn.f: Posting reminder signs near sinks can increase how often staff clean their hands.

E.w: The topic sentence says that hand washing prevents the spread of infection. The sentence about hand dryers shares words such as hands and hospitals, but its point is reducing waste, not preventing infection, so it breaks the paragraph's unity.

n.a: This is the topic sentence that the rest of the paragraph supports.
n.b: This explains how germs spread from patient to patient, which shows why hand washing matters.
n.c: This explains how washing removes germs, direct support for the topic sentence.
n.e: This gives another way to clean hands, which supports the goal of preventing infection.
n.f: This describes a way to make hand cleaning more frequent, which supports the topic sentence.

E.q: A student writing a lab report adds prefixes to base words. Which word correctly keeps every letter of both the prefix and the root?
o: disatisfied
imature
unnecessary
mispell
E.w: Adding a prefix does not change the spelling of the root: un + necessary = "unnecessary", with both n's kept.

n.0: Dis + satisfied keeps both s's: "dissatisfied".
n.1: Im + mature keeps both m's: "immature".
n.3: Mis + spell keeps both s's: "misspell".

E.q: A patient-education leaflet uses each of the words below. Based on their suffixes, which of the words are adjectives? Select all that apply.
o: rapidly
donor
treatable
painful
nervous
sterilize
E.w: -ful (full of), -able (able to be) and -ous (having, full of) form adjectives: painful, treatable, nervous.

n.0: -ly added to an adjective forms an adverb (rapidly).
n.1: -or forms a noun naming a person (donor = one who gives).
n.5: -ize forms verbs meaning to make (sterilize = to make sterile).

E.q: A nursing student is reviewing sentence structure before the TEAS. Which of the following is a complex sentence?
o: Although she studied all week, Rosa felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week and felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week, yet she felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week; she still felt nervous before the exam.
E.w: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. "Although she studied all week" is dependent (it begins with a subordinating conjunction); "Rosa felt nervous before the exam" is independent.

n.1: One subject with two verbs (studied and felt) is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by a comma and "yet" make a compound sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon make a compound sentence.

E.q: During morning rounds, the nurse recorded a patient's pulse of 48 beats per minute and described it in the chart as bradycardia. Based on its prefix, what does bradycardia mean?
o: A painful heartbeat
An irregular heart rate
A slow heart rate
A fast heart rate
E.w: brady- means slow and cardi/o means heart, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate (a pulse of 48 fits).

n.0: Pain would come from a suffix such as -algia or -dynia; brady- describes speed, not pain.
n.1: Neither brady- nor cardia refers to rhythm; an irregular rhythm is an arrhythmia.
n.3: A fast heart rate is tachycardia; tachy- means fast, the opposite of brady-.

E.q: A reporter is writing about a city official's school visit. Which version of the sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: Last Winter, the mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the Mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the mayor visited Northside high school on Oak avenue.
E.w: Two rules apply. Proper names of a school and a street are capitalized in full (Northside High School, Oak Avenue), but a season and a title used without a name (the mayor) are lowercase.

n.0: Seasons are common nouns, so "winter" is lowercase.
n.1: "Mayor" is not followed by a name, so it is lowercase.
n.3: "High School" and "Avenue" are parts of proper names, so they are capitalized.

E.q: After a fall from a ladder, a construction worker had a CT scan that ruled out intracranial bleeding. Based on its word parts, where would intracranial bleeding occur?
o: Between the skull bones
Around the outer skull
Below the skull
Inside the skull
E.w: intra- means within and crani/o means skull, so intracranial means inside the skull.

n.0: Between is inter-, the look-alike prefix.
n.1: Around is peri- or circum-.
n.2: Below is sub- or hypo-.

E.q: Read the sentence from a hospital newsletter: "The physician noted that the patient's hemorrage had stopped before the anesthesia wore off." Which word in the sentence is misspelled?
o: physician
anesthesia
patient's
hemorrage
E.w: The correct spelling is "hemorrhage", with r-r-h; the rh comes from the Greek word part -rrhage (bursting forth).

n.0: "Physician" is spelled correctly.
n.1: "Anesthesia" is the correct US spelling (UK: anaesthesia).
n.2: "Patient's" is the correct singular possessive of patient.

E.q: Read the sentence from a shift report: "When the shift ended, Maya charted her notes, and Luis restocked the supply cart." Which statement correctly describes the structure of this sentence?
o: It is compound-complex because it has two independent clauses and a dependent clause.
It is complex because it opens with the dependent clause "When the shift ended."
It is compound because two independent clauses are joined by a comma and "and."
It is simple because it has one subject performing a series of related actions.
E.w: The sentence has two independent clauses (Maya charted her notes; Luis restocked the supply cart) and one dependent clause (When the shift ended), so it is compound-complex.

n.1: A complex sentence has only one independent clause; this one has two.
n.2: A compound sentence has no dependent clause; this one also has "When the shift ended".
n.3: There are two subjects (Maya, Luis) with their own verbs, so there are two independent clauses, not one.
